problems.name: Leakage, loss and bursts

doe.pullWhy: Atom loss limits neutral-atom circuits from the first deep logical circuit, IonQ's 2026 qLDPC run discarded 19% to 75% of shots on detected leakage, and leakage and bursts set the noise floor First-generation runs must stay under.
doe.verifyWhy: The noise floor and logical error rates are direct V&V quantities.
doe.vv: Logical noise floor, leakage population, loss-adjusted logical error, uptime.

problems.title: Autonomous Calibration and Drift Control at 10^3-10^5 Qubits
problems.one_liner: Keeping thousands to millions of qubits calibrated and drift-free during operation, using AI/RL agents, dependency graphs, and frequency allocation instead of manual tuning.
problems.statement: As processors scale from hundreds to 10^3-10^5+ physical qubits, calibration cannot stay a human-supervised, mostly offline procedure. Parameter counts grow faster than engineering time, frequency crowding and two-level-system defects drift daily, and long QEC runs need calibration interleaved with logic rather than done once at bring-up. The problem spans four linked pieces: representing calibration dependencies as a graph so routines schedule and re-trigger automatically; allocating qubit frequencies and control parameters to avoid crosstalk and defect collisions at array scale; tracking drift in situ during QEC cycles and feeding corrections back without halting logic; and using reinforcement-learning or language-model agents to propose and validate control changes with little human review. A solved version of this problem produces a demonstrated closed loop, from bring-up through many hours of unattended operation, that holds logical error rate and the error-suppression factor Lambda within a stated tolerance at 10^4 or more qubits, reporting calibration time per qubit and uptime as auditable numbers rather than vendor claims.

anchors.item: RL agent tunes 1,000+ control parameters live during QEC from syndrome data; d=7 logical error 7.72e-4/cycle, ~20% lower logical error, up to 3.5x drift stability, ~40,000 parameters explored in simulation
anchors.dependency: Must scale from ~1,000 hardware parameters to calibration-at-scale (10^4-10^6 qubits)

anchors.item: Lists calibration-at-scale (10^4-10^6 qubits) as a needed capability on its public roadmap
anchors.dependency: No published method yet demonstrated beyond hundreds of qubits

anchors.item: Nighthawk (120 qubits, 2025) and the 2029 Starling target (100 million gates on 200 logical qubits) require calibrating long-range couplers across chiplets/modules
anchors.dependency: Multi-chip qLDPC architecture needs coupler calibration to scale across modules first

anchors.item: AI agent (Anthropic's Claude) wrote and validated laser-lock recovery control logic; 695/700 successful recoveries, most under 6-14 seconds
anchors.dependency: Subsystem-level automation is a precursor to unattended, multi-thousand-atom array calibration

criteria_why.C1: Scaling closed-loop control theory (DAGs, RL, drift estimation) to 10^5 qubits is open research, not routine engineering.
criteria_why.C2: Logical error rate, Lambda, calibration time per qubit, and uptime are all directly measurable per run.
criteria_why.C3: Open frameworks (Qibocal, QUAlibrate) let outside groups contribute once released, but real hardware access stays limited.
criteria_why.C4: No shared theory unifies DAG scheduling, RL agents, and drift tracking across superconducting and atom-array platforms.
criteria_why.C5: Naturally stages from single-qubit routines to DAG scheduling to closed-loop RL to cross-platform generalization.
criteria_why.C6: Proving stability or convergence of autonomous calibration loops at scale lacks general results; work is mostly empirical.

problems.access_note: Algorithm prototyping is possible in simulation, but validating drift and defect models needs real qubit hardware.

metrics.name: Calibration time per qubit
metrics.def: Wall-clock time to bring one qubit or routine to spec, amortized over array size (seconds/qubit or minutes for full-chip bring-up).
metrics.sota: QUAlibrate reports cutting full-system calibration from hours to minutes (Quantum Machines, 2025)

metrics.name: System uptime / fault recovery time
metrics.def: Fraction of time the processor runs logic versus recalibrating, or time to recover from a detected fault.
metrics.sota: QuEra's Claude-built laser-lock recovery fixed faults in under 6-14 seconds across 695/700 trials (QuEra, Aug 2026)

metrics.name: Logical error rate per cycle under drift
metrics.def: Logical error probability per QEC cycle, tracked over a run; degradation over time signals uncompensated drift.
metrics.sota: Google's RL agent held ~20% lower logical error and up to 3.5x more stable drift at d=7 (7.72e-4/cycle) versus a static baseline (Google, Nature, 2026)

metrics.name: Relaxation-rate / Lambda drift tracking
metrics.def: Continuous tracking of T1/T2 or the error-suppression factor Lambda as a live measure of calibration staleness.
metrics.sota: Real-time adaptive tracking of fluctuating relaxation rates demonstrated on superconducting qubits (Berritta et al., Phys. Rev. X, 2025-26)

stages.name: Baseline routines and dependency graphs
stages.goal: Establish per-qubit calibration routines and their dependency order for automatic bring-up.
stages.exit: Full-chip calibration completes automatically without manual reordering of routines.
stages.note: Solved for single-chip superconducting processors since Kelly et al. 2018.

stages.name: Open, reusable calibration software stacks
stages.goal: Build vendor-neutral, open-source frameworks any lab can run calibration routines through.
stages.exit: A framework runs full bring-up and tune-up on independent hardware without vendor code.
stages.note: Qibocal, Qibolab, and QUAlibrate now run across multiple non-vendor labs (2023-2025).

stages.name: Frequency/parameter allocation and defect avoidance at scale
stages.goal: Assign frequencies and control parameters across hundreds-to-thousands of qubits avoiding crosstalk and defects.
stages.exit: Demonstrated collision-aware allocation and defect-aware tuning on a 100+ qubit array with measured yield.
stages.note: Frequency-allocation algorithms and ML-based defect detection shown to hundreds of qubits (2023-2026).

stages.name: Closed-loop RL/agentic calibration during operation
stages.goal: Let an RL or language-model agent tune parameters continuously while QEC logic runs.
stages.exit: A closed loop sustains improved logical error or Lambda over a multi-hour run with published numbers.
stages.note: Google's RL agent (2026) is the first such hardware result; QuEra automated one subsystem the same year.

stages.name: General theory and cross-platform generalization at 10^4-10^6 qubits
stages.goal: Find a framework or theory that provably scales calibration and drift control across hardware platforms.
stages.exit: A published scaling law or provable guarantee for calibration overhead at 10^4+ qubits, validated on hardware.
stages.note: No platform has published autonomous calibration results above roughly 1,000 qubits; theory is largely absent.

IBM.headline: TLS and coupler research underway; no published closed-loop demo at scale.
IBM.summary: IBM's roadmap needs calibrated long-range couplers across chiplets for Nighthawk (120 qubits, 2025) and the 2029 Starling target of 100 million gates on 200 logical qubits. Community and IBM-adjacent work has produced machine-learning two-level-system detection and site-specific frequency tuning around defects (2025-2026), but no published IBM demonstration yet closes the calibration loop autonomously during a live, multi-hour QEC run at scale.

Google.headline: First hardware demo of an RL agent tuning parameters live during QEC.
Google.summary: Google's Nature paper (July 2026) shows an RL agent tuning over 1,000 control parameters from syndrome data during operation, reaching 7.72e-4 logical error per cycle at distance 7, about 20% lower logical error, and up to 3.5x more stable drift than static calibration, exploring roughly 40,000 parameters in simulation. Google's roadmap separately lists calibration-at-scale (10^4-10^6 qubits) as a needed, unmet capability, building on earlier dependency-graph (2018) and gate-optimization (2024) calibration work.

QuEra.headline: AI agent automated one subsystem's recovery; full-array calibration not yet shown.
QuEra.summary: In August 2026 QuEra reported that an AI agent built with Anthropic's Claude wrote and validated control logic that recovers laser lock in its neutral-atom systems, succeeding in 695 of 700 timed trials, most under 6 seconds, with zero false positives and a fivefold reduction in laser noise, matching experienced manual tuning. This automates one calibration subsystem, a precursor to full autonomous array calibration, building on Harvard/QuEra's continuous 3,000-atom operation reported in Nature in 2025.

IonQ.headline: Small-scale Oxford Ionics hardware shows sparse automated calibration; no AI or RL agents.
IonQ.summary: Oxford Ionics, now part of IonQ, reported a seven-zone all-electronic trap in which only the motional frequency was recalibrated by an automated routine (about one automated calibration per gate parameter per day) over a 60-hour run, with average fidelity drift near 1e-4 per day. A company blog argues the architecture was designed so a 10,000-qubit machine has the same calibration overhead as a 10-qubit one. No machine-learning or reinforcement-learning calibration, and no data at large scale, has been published.
IonQ.gateWhy: IonQ's 2027 single-chip target of 10,000 physical qubits relies on calibration overhead not growing with qubit count; 2026 systems of 100-256 qubits can be calibrated conventionally.

Community.headline: Open frameworks plus agentic and ML calibration research are maturing quickly.
Community.summary: Academic and vendor-neutral groups have built open calibration stacks (Qibocal and Qibolab from the Qibo collaboration; Quantum Machines' QUAlibrate) and shown language-model-driven bring-up: self-driving-lab agents in 2024, a 112-qubit language-agent bring-up in 2026, and LLM-assisted experiment design in 2026. Parallel work targets scaling bottlenecks: ML defect detection and site-specific tuning, frequency-collision and crosstalk-allocation algorithms, active-learning gate calibration, real-time relaxation-rate tracking, and early theory for provably efficient self-calibrating fault tolerance. Q-CTRL and NVIDIA are commercializing autonomous calibration with partners including QuantWare, TreQ, and Equal1 (2025-2026).

overall.headline: Real closed-loop demos exist at hundreds of qubits; scaling to 10^4-10^6 remains unsolved.
overall.summary: Between 2024 and 2026 the field moved from graph-based bring-up automation (2018) and open calibration software to real closed-loop demonstrations: Google's RL agent tuning over 1,000 parameters live during a distance-7 QEC run (Nature, July 2026), and QuEra's Claude-built laser-lock recovery (August 2026, 695 of 700 successes). IBM's roadmap depends on similar automation for multi-chip coupler calibration but has not published a comparable closed-loop demonstration. All current results sit at hundreds, not thousands-to-millions, of qubits; frequency-allocation, defect-avoidance, and cross-platform theory for 10^4-10^6-qubit calibration remain largely open.

gaps.gap: No published autonomous calibration demo above roughly 1,000 qubits
gaps.why_hard: Control-system bandwidth, latency, and dependency-graph complexity do not obviously scale linearly, and few groups have hardware this large to test on.
gaps.entry_point: Benchmark existing RL and DAG calibration methods in simulation at 10^3-10^4 simulated qubits with realistic noise to locate bottlenecks before hardware exists.

gaps.gap: No shared calibration theory across superconducting, atom-array, and spin platforms
gaps.why_hard: Each modality fails differently (two-level-system defects versus atom loss versus charge noise), resisting one shared abstraction or scheduler.
gaps.entry_point: Define a common calibration-dependency-graph representation that different hardware backends can plug into, then compare RL/active-learning agents on top of it.

gaps.gap: No agreed metric for calibration overhead at scale
gaps.why_hard: Vendors report different quantities (minutes to calibrate, uptime, success rate), making cross-platform comparison currently impossible.
gaps.entry_point: Publish a small open benchmark, similar to Metriq, that logs calibration time, uptime, and post-calibration Lambda for any backend.

doe.pullWhy: DOE judges progress by whether a system 'can operate reliably, repeatedly, and at sufficient throughput'. Machines with 10,000 or more qubits cannot be kept in tune by hand.
doe.verifyWhy: Measurable with access, but today mostly inside each vendor; DOE's V&V access would make it checkable.
doe.vv: Uptime, recovery time, and logical error under drift.

problems.title: Inter-module links and distributed fault tolerance
problems.one_liner: Connecting error-corrected modules through noisy, slow links and running fault-tolerant logical operations across them at scale.
problems.statement: Fault-tolerant architectures beyond a single chip or cryostat must connect separately encoded modules through physical links — chip-to-chip couplers, microwave cables between cryostats, or optical fiber — that are far noisier and slower than intra-module operations. The problem is making logical operations (lattice surgery, teleported gates, entanglement distillation) fault-tolerant across such links: deriving thresholds for combined bulk-and-link error rates, designing entanglement generation and purification protocols that meet the rate and fidelity a given code needs, and scheduling and compiling circuits so scarce inter-module entanglement is used efficiently. 'Solved' means a validated theory connecting link fidelity and rate to logical error rate for realistic codes, hardware links that meet those requirements at multi-module scale, and compilers that keep logical algorithms running efficiently across dozens to thousands of linked modules — matching what IBM's Cockatoo and Starling, Google's networked Milestone 6, and modular photonic or neutral-atom systems will require between 2027 and 2031.

anchors.item: Cockatoo (2027): links Kookaburra modules using dedicated 'L-couplers'
anchors.dependency: Requires quantum inter-module coupler hardware plus cross-module logical operations

anchors.item: IBM-Cisco partnership to network quantum computers (announced Nov 2025)
anchors.dependency: Classical/quantum networking effort supporting multi-computer scale-out

anchors.item: Milestone 6: make, connect and control about 1,000,000 physical qubits
anchors.dependency: Needs inter-chip interconnect fidelity and control density at million-qubit scale

anchors.item: Acquired Atlantic Quantum (2025) for cold-stage integrated control electronics
anchors.dependency: Reduces wiring overhead needed to connect and control million-qubit systems

anchors.item: Gigaquop system (2028-2029): >1,000 logical qubits and >20,000 atoms in one processing core
anchors.dependency: Targets single-core scale first; multi-core/module linking is the follow-on scale-out step

criteria_why.C1: Requires new threshold theory, distillation protocols and cross-module scheduling, not just faster links.
criteria_why.C2: Logical error rate versus link fidelity/rate is directly simulable and independently measurable on hardware.
criteria_why.C3: Threshold and lattice-surgery papers already show many independent groups building on shared noisy-link models.
criteria_why.C4: Two-module threshold theory is mature (Nickerson, de Bone, Ramette) but no single cross-architecture standard covers 3+ modules.
criteria_why.C5: Splits into threshold theory, distillation protocols, two-module demos, multi-module scheduling, and at-scale networks.
criteria_why.C6: Distributed fault-tolerance proofs for heterogeneous, noisy-linked qLDPC/surface-code networks are hard but tractable case by case.

problems.access_note: Two-module demonstrations exist in custom labs (Oxford, IBM, Harvard/AWS); no public cloud offers linked multi-module access.

metrics.name: Inter-module logical/teleported gate fidelity
metrics.def: Fidelity of a two-qubit gate (e.g. a teleported CZ) executed across the physical link joining two modules.
metrics.sota: 86.2(9)% teleported CZ fidelity between photonically linked trapped-ion modules (Main et al., Oxford, 2025).

metrics.name: Remote entanglement generation rate
metrics.def: Rate (pairs/second) at which the link produces usable entangled pairs between modules at a stated fidelity.
metrics.sota: 9.7 pairs/s at 96.89(8)% Bell fidelity over a ~2 m optical link (Main et al., 2025); up to 1 Hz over 35 km of deployed telecom fiber for networked memory nodes (Knaut et al., 2024).

metrics.name: Interface-to-bulk error ratio at threshold
metrics.def: Ratio of the link (interface) error rate to the intra-module (bulk) error rate tolerated at the fault-tolerance threshold.
metrics.sota: About 14x higher interface noise tolerated than bulk noise (roughly 10% interface, 1% bulk) in a modular surface-code scheme (Ramette et al., 2023/24).

metrics.name: Entanglement-rate-to-decoherence-rate threshold
metrics.def: Minimum ratio of entanglement-generation rate to qubit decoherence rate needed to keep a distributed code below threshold.
metrics.sota: Ratio of about 400 required under realistic NV-center noise models, roughly 3x stricter than earlier estimates (de Bone et al., 2024).

stages.name: Threshold theory and foundational link infrastructure
stages.goal: Establish fault-tolerance threshold theory for noisy links plus the physical/control primitives linking depends on.
stages.exit: Published threshold curves (bulk error vs. link error/rate) validated by simulation, plus a demonstrated entangling or control primitive.
stages.note: Seminal noisy-network thresholds (2013) extended to realistic surface-code and NV-center models by 2024; atom-transport and control-electronics primitives exist.

stages.name: Entanglement generation and distillation protocols
stages.goal: Design purification/distillation schemes that reach the fidelity and rate a given threshold needs.
stages.exit: A protocol demonstrating constant-rate or otherwise scalable distillation meeting a stated threshold.
stages.note: Constant-rate distillation and modular architecture/entanglement-scheme comparisons published 2024-2025.

stages.name: Two-module hardware demonstrations
stages.goal: Demonstrate a teleported gate or logical operation between two physically separate modules.
stages.exit: A real inter-module link running a deterministic logical or physical operation with reported fidelity.
stages.note: IBM, Oxford, Harvard/AWS and Xanadu each reported concrete two-module or multi-chip link fidelities by 2025; IonQ reported a further link in 2026.

stages.name: Cross-module fault-tolerant operations at small scale
stages.goal: Extend lattice surgery or transversal logical operations across three or more modules with heterogeneous link noise.
stages.exit: A simulated or small hardware demo of a fault-tolerant logical operation spanning >=3 modules.
stages.note: 2026 papers simulate heterogeneous-distance lattice surgery and transversal distributed CNOTs; no hardware demo yet.

stages.name: Link-aware compilation and scheduling
stages.goal: Build compilers that jointly optimize qubit mapping and scheduling around scarce inter-module entanglement.
stages.exit: A compiler demonstrating a validated reduction in inter-module operations or entanglement use on multi-module benchmarks.
stages.note: Early link-placement compilers report double-digit-percent fidelity and SWAP-count improvements on small benchmarks.

stages.name: At-scale modular fault-tolerant network
stages.goal: Operate tens to thousands of linked, error-corrected modules running roadmap-scale algorithms.
stages.exit: A vendor demonstrates a networked fault-tolerant system across >=3 real modules meeting a target application's error budget.
stages.note: IBM's Cockatoo (2027) and Google's Milestone 6 both target this regime but no public multi-module result exists yet.

IBM.headline: Two QPUs linked classically (2024); quantum L-couplers due 2027
IBM.summary: IBM linked two 127-qubit Eagle processors with a real-time classical link and circuit-cutting, building a 134-qubit graph state spanning both devices and detecting bipartite entanglement across all edges at 99% confidence (Carrera Vazquez et al., Nature 2024). This link is classical, not quantum-coherent; IBM's roadmap plans genuine quantum interconnection via dedicated 'L-couplers' linking Kookaburra modules in Cockatoo (2027), and it announced a quantum-networking partnership with Cisco in late 2025.

Google.headline: Targets ~1M-qubit interconnect via Milestone 6; little public link data
Google.summary: Google frames Milestone 6 as making, connecting and controlling about 1,000,000 physical qubits, and acquired Atlantic Quantum in 2025 for cold-stage integrated control electronics meant to cut wiring overhead at that scale. Beyond this control-stack move, no Google-authored inter-module entanglement-link or cross-chip logical-operation result with reported fidelity or rate numbers was found; module-linking research relevant to Google's architecture currently comes mostly from academic groups.

QuEra.headline: Theory paper derives optical-link FT thresholds; no hardware inter-module demo yet
QuEra.summary: QuEra's gigaquop roadmap (2028-2029) targets over 1,000 logical qubits and more than 20,000 atoms inside a single processing core rather than linking separate cores, so no public inter-module link fidelity or rate numbers exist yet. The company's core primitive, coherent transport of entangled atom arrays between processing zones (Bluvstein et al., Nature 2022), is the movement-based mechanism a future multi-core or multi-chamber link would need to extend, but that extension has not been published. A 2024 Harvard/MIT theory paper (Sinclair, Ramette, Grinkemeyer, Bluvstein, Lukin, Vuletić) derives fault-tolerance requirements for photonically interconnected neutral-atom modules, needing local Rydberg-gate error below 1% and non-local Bell-pair error below 10%, though this remains simulation/theory rather than a hardware link demonstration.

IonQ.headline: Duke-IonQ three-node photonic entanglement and a two-system link; no logical operations across modules.
IonQ.summary: A June 2026 Duke-IonQ preprint reports a three-node network of single barium-138 ions entangled through photonic links into a GHZ state, without post-selection or local two-qubit gates: fidelity 0.841 to 0.881 at 0.095 events per second, nodes about 2 m apart. In April 2026 IonQ announced photonic interconnection of two commercial trapped-ion systems, without published rates. These are physical-level link results; no fault-tolerant logical operation across modules has been published, and the roadmap brings networked chips online in 2028.
IonQ.gateWhy: IonQ's blueprint fits 100+ logical qubits on one chip, so networked modules are needed only for its 2028-2030 steps (1,600 to 80,000 logical qubits).

Community.headline: Most active: threshold theory, distillation, and real two-module demos
Community.summary: Academic groups lead most demonstrated progress. Oxford's ion-trap group ran the first deterministic distributed algorithm over a photonic link (86.2% teleported-gate fidelity, Main et al., Nature 2025); a Harvard/AWS team networked diamond memory nodes over 35 km of deployed fiber (Knaut et al., 2024); and Xanadu networked 35 photonic chips into Aurora (2025). MIT, Delft and Harvard groups built noisy-link threshold and distillation theory, NC State, Argonne and Fordham published 2025-26 cross-module surgery and link-aware compilation work, and IonQ reported a first photonic interconnect between two commercial systems (2026).

overall.headline: Two-module links proven; multi-module fault-tolerant networks remain simulated
overall.summary: Since 2024, several groups have demonstrated real physical links between two error-corrected or near-error-corrected modules: IBM's classically linked 142-qubit Eagle pair, Oxford's photonically linked ion-trap modules, a Harvard/AWS telecom-networked memory-node pair, and Xanadu's 35-chip Aurora system, each with reported fidelities and rates. Threshold and distillation theory for two noisy-linked modules is mature (Nickerson, Ramette, de Bone, Pattison), and 2026 papers extend it to three-plus modules and qLDPC codes in simulation, but no vendor has yet shown a fault-tolerant logical operation spanning three or more real, separately encoded modules.

gaps.gap: No fault-tolerant operation demonstrated across >=3 real modules
gaps.why_hard: Needs simultaneous gains in link rate and fidelity, synchronized multi-module control, and new real-time multi-module decoders.
gaps.entry_point: Simulate a 3-module lattice-surgery circuit in Stim using published link-noise parameters (Ramette/de Bone) and compare against 2026 heterogeneous-distance schemes.

gaps.gap: No shared cost model linking link rate/fidelity to logical error across architectures
gaps.why_hard: Ion-trap, superconducting, photonic and neutral-atom links have very different rate, fidelity and loss tradeoffs that do not transfer directly.
gaps.entry_point: Build an open benchmark converting (link rate, link fidelity, bulk error) triples from each platform into a predicted distributed logical error rate.

gaps.gap: Link-aware compilers remain early and platform-specific
gaps.why_hard: Optimal scheduling depends on a specific coupler topology and noise profile, so results like InterPlace do not generalize automatically.
gaps.entry_point: Extend an existing link-aware compiler to a second hardware topology and to qLDPC-code circuits, not only surface-code benchmarks.

problems.note: IBM's 2024 link is classical (circuit cutting with real-time classical communication). Quantum L-couplers are scheduled for Cockatoo in 2027.
problems.name: Fault tolerance across modules

doe.pullWhy: IBM's 200-logical-qubit Starling is built from linked modules, IonQ links two chips from 2028 and Google's million-qubit milestone needs links. QuEra plans one processing core through 1,000 logical qubits.
doe.verifyWhy: Logical gate fidelity across modules is a V&V quantity.
doe.vv: Inter-module logical gate fidelity and remote entanglement rate.

problems.title: Early-FT application instances with rigorous classical baselines
problems.one_liner: Find concrete 100-1,000-logical-qubit problem instances in chemistry, materials, or optimization that beat the strongest classical baseline at matched accuracy.
problems.statement: Roadmaps (IBM Starling, QuEra Libra/gigaquop) target 100-1,000 logical qubits and 1e6-1e9 logical operations by 2028-2031, but almost no concrete problem instance at that scale has been shown to beat the best classical method at matched accuracy. Solving this means selecting specific instances - a named molecule's ground-state energy, a materials Hamiltonian, an optimization instance, a cryptanalytic target, or a structured-inference problem - and pairing each with the strongest classical baseline achievable today, not an outdated one, evaluated at the same accuracy the quantum method claims. 'Solved' means an instance clears Grand Challenge Stages II-III: a resource-estimated quantum approach plus an actively contested classical baseline, ideally with independent replication, so the advantage claim is falsifiable and has survived good-faith attempts to beat it classically - the way IBM's Quantum Advantage Tracker and Google's Quantum Echoes and DQI results are now being tested in public.

anchors.item: Starling: 200 logical qubits, 1e8 gates - first large-scale fault-tolerant computer
anchors.dependency: Sets the qubit/gate-count window candidate P13 instances must fit inside

anchors.item: Grand Challenge of Quantum Applications: 5-stage framework, no application yet at Stage V
anchors.dependency: Defines the Stage II-III bar (beyond-classical instance) P13 instances must clear

anchors.item: Gidney RSA-2048 estimate: under 1,000,000 noisy qubits, under 1 week
anchors.dependency: A concrete cryptanalysis instance in the exact resource-counted format P13 wants replicated elsewhere

anchors.item: Libra megaquop system on Amazon Braket: >256 logical qubits, ~1e-6 error
anchors.dependency: First cloud-accessible platform sized for testing candidate P13 instances

criteria_why.C1: Needs new algorithms/instances proving beyond-classical performance at fixed accuracy, not routine engineering
criteria_why.C2: Cost-at-matched-accuracy is computable, but the 'best classical baseline' keeps shifting as methods improve
criteria_why.C3: Once instance and baseline are fixed, any group can attempt an improved classical or quantum solver
criteria_why.C4: No agreed methodology exists for what counts as a rigorous, non-stale classical baseline across domains
criteria_why.C5: Splits naturally into instance selection, baseline construction, and independent verification stages
criteria_why.C6: Proving no faster classical algorithm exists is often as hard as the original quantum contribution

problems.access_note: The 100-1,000 logical-qubit target regime does not exist yet; work is classical resource estimation plus small early-FT/NISQ hardware pilots

metrics.name: Quantum-vs-best-classical cost ratio at fixed accuracy
metrics.def: Wall-clock or gate cost of the best known classical method reaching a target physical quantity at a stated accuracy, divided by the quantum resource estimate for the same accuracy
metrics.sota: No chemistry/materials instance has a settled ratio; IBM's peaked-circuit candidate saw its classical-cost estimate fall from ~4 months to seconds between Dec 2025 and Feb 2026 (IBM Quantum Advantage Tracker)

metrics.name: Physical-qubit count for a named chemistry target at chemical accuracy
metrics.def: Physical qubits (of a stated technology) needed to reach chemical accuracy on a specific molecule's ground-state energy, from an end-to-end compiled estimate
metrics.sota: ~99,000 cat qubits and 78-99 hours estimated runtime for FeMoco/P450 (Alice & Bob LDPC-cat estimator, 2023-2025), about 27x fewer physical qubits than an equivalent transmon-plus-surface-code estimate

metrics.name: Speedup exponent for structured-inference problems
metrics.def: Ratio of classical to quantum query/gate complexity for a planted-inference-type problem, as a function of instance size
metrics.sota: Proven nearly-quartic (4th power) speedup for Tensor PCA-type planted inference via the Kikuchi method, using only logarithmically many qubits (Schmidhuber, O'Donnell, Kothari & Babbush, PRX 15, 021077, 2025)

metrics.name: Hardware-demonstrated speedup vs. classical-simulation cost
metrics.def: Measured runtime of a physics-simulation task on real hardware, divided by the estimated classical-supercomputer runtime for the same task at the same fidelity
metrics.sota: Google's Quantum Echoes: ~2 hours on the 65-103-qubit Willow chip vs. an estimated 3.2 years per data point on the Frontier supercomputer (~13,000x), while a companion NMR verification experiment is explicitly 'not yet beyond classical' (Mi, Kechedzhi et al., Nature, 2025)

stages.name: Baseline infrastructure
stages.goal: Define candidate domains, simulators, and what counts as evidence for advantage
stages.exit: A public survey classifies end-to-end resource complexity for major candidate algorithms
stages.note: Dalzell et al. (2023) and Lee et al. (2023) establish this for broad algorithm classes and chemistry specifically

stages.name: Candidate instances and algorithms proposed
stages.goal: Name concrete instances or algorithms with a claimed quantum edge
stages.exit: At least one named instance per domain (chemistry, optimization, materials) has a published resource estimate
stages.note: FeMoco/P450, Fermi-Hubbard, DQI-solved optimization instances, and Quantum-Echoes-style physics tasks all exist, but coverage is uneven across domains

stages.name: Early fault-tolerant circuit techniques
stages.goal: Develop circuit-depth-efficient algorithms usable before full fault tolerance arrives
stages.exit: An early-FT algorithm is tested in simulation or on hardware with realistic noise, not just asymptotically
stages.note: The QCELS/QET-U family (Lin & Tong 2021-2022; Ding et al. 2023) is developed and partly tested in practice

stages.name: Adversarial classical-baseline stress-testing
stages.goal: Actively try to dequantize or classically match proposed advantage claims
stages.exit: At least one dedicated classical-algorithm effort attempts to close the gap for each candidate instance
stages.note: A dequantization tradition exists (Tang 2018) and IBM's tracker shows classical baselines collapsing in near-real time for peaked circuits, but this loop is not yet routine for chemistry/materials instances

stages.name: Independent, replicated beyond-classical demonstration
stages.goal: Reach an instance where multiple independent groups agree quantum wins at matched accuracy, at the 100-1,000 logical-qubit / 1e6-1e9 op scale
stages.exit: At least two independent teams replicate a beyond-classical result at matched accuracy on the same instance
stages.note: No instance has cleared Grand Challenge Stage III with independent replication; public claims (e.g. IBM, April/July 2026) remain unverified by outside teams

stages.name: General theory of early-FT quantum advantage
stages.goal: A predictive framework for which problem classes show real, non-asymptotic advantage in the 1e6-1e9 operation regime
stages.exit: A theory correctly predicts advantage or no-advantage for at least three new problem classes before resource estimation is run
stages.note: Only qualitative guidance exists (avoid quadratic-only speedups; count physical run-time, not query complexity); no predictive theory yet

IBM.headline: Runs a public, crowdsourced classical-vs-quantum tracker
IBM.summary: IBM's Quantum Advantage Tracker lets outside teams (Flatiron Institute, BlueQubit, Algorithmiq, Caltech, Los Alamos) submit quantum and classical results on candidate instances such as peaked circuits. BlueQubit's December 2025 run used about 4,000-5,000 two-qubit gates on IBM hardware in under 12 minutes, while the best classical estimate for the same task fell from about four months to seconds by February 2026 as methods improved - a concrete case of a claimed edge narrowing in public within ten weeks.

Google.headline: Hardware demo (Quantum Echoes) plus new theory (DQI, Grand Challenge staging)
Google.summary: Google's 65-103-qubit Willow chip ran the Quantum Echoes OTOC algorithm about 13,000x faster than an estimated classical run on the Frontier supercomputer (Mi, Kechedzhi et al., Nature, 2025), though a companion NMR verification experiment concedes it is 'not yet beyond classical.' Google researchers also introduced Decoded Quantum Interferometry for optimization (Jordan et al., 2024) and published a five-stage 'Grand Challenge' framework (Nov 2025) in which no application yet reaches Stage V.

QuEra.headline: Roadmap names target platforms; no named P13 instance published yet
QuEra.summary: QuEra's June 2026 roadmap targets a >256-logical-qubit 'Libra' megaquop system on Amazon Braket by 2028 (about 1e-6 logical error) and a >1,000-logical-qubit 'gigaquop' system by 2028-2029 (about 1e-9), pitched explicitly as platforms for early beyond-classical applications. Its FTQC Founders Circle invites partner organizations to co-design candidate applications (the BB-STAR case study), but as of September 2026 no peer-reviewed QuEra application instance with a matched classical baseline at P13 scale has been published.

IonQ.headline: Resource estimates for Heisenberg simulation and Shor; no classical-beating claim published.
IonQ.summary: On its Walking Cat design IonQ estimates a 100-site Heisenberg-model simulation to chemical accuracy at about one month on roughly 10,000 physical qubits (162 logical qubits), and Shor's algorithm on 30-bit numbers at about 13,000 physical qubits in under a day. Both are simulation-based estimates for IonQ's own architecture, and neither is presented as beating the best classical methods. IonQ's pre-fault-tolerant application papers, such as a 32-qubit nuclear-physics simulation, give no fault-tolerant resource estimates. No early-fault-tolerant advantage instance has been demonstrated.
IonQ.gateWhy: 100+ logical qubits with 10^5 hard operations (First-generation tier) is the scale at which IonQ's own estimates place its first applications.

Community.headline: Broadest activity: algorithm design, dequantization, and cross-lab benchmarking
Community.summary: Academic and industry groups drive most progress: Babbush et al. (2021) argued for moving beyond quadratic speedups; Lee et al. (2023, Nature Communications) audited the evidence for chemistry advantage; Kan & Symons (IBM, 2024) produced Fermi-Hubbard resource estimates; Schmidhuber, O'Donnell, Kothari & Babbush (2025) proved a quartic speedup for planted inference; Alice & Bob published cat-qubit FeMoco/P450 estimates; and Tang's 2018 dequantization result exemplifies a long tradition of narrowing claimed gaps. DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative is separately building an independent verification process, with first milestones due late 2026.

overall.headline: Ingredients exist separately; no instance has independent, matched-accuracy replication
overall.summary: As of September 2026, the pieces for P13 are maturing in parallel but have not converged: resource estimates for FeMoco/P450/Fermi-Hubbard exist across several qubit technologies, early-fault-tolerant algorithms are being tested in practice, and Google's Quantum Echoes shows a roughly 13,000x hardware speedup on one physics task while its own NMR companion experiment admits it is not yet beyond classical. IBM's community tracker shows classical baselines can collapse from months to seconds within weeks. No chemistry, materials, or optimization instance has yet reached Grand Challenge Stage III with an independently replicated, accuracy-matched classical baseline.

gaps.gap: No standard for a 'rigorous' classical baseline across domains
gaps.why_hard: Classical heuristics, tensor networks, and dequantization all improve unpredictably, so a published baseline can collapse soon after
gaps.entry_point: Extend IBM's open, timestamped Advantage-Tracker model from circuit sampling to at least one chemistry or optimization instance

gaps.gap: FeMoco/P450-style estimates disagree by orders of magnitude across architectures
gaps.why_hard: Superconducting, cat-qubit, and photonic estimates use different noise models, compilers, and accuracy targets, so the numbers are not directly comparable
gaps.entry_point: Publish one molecule's resource estimate through two independent compilation pipelines (e.g. Qualtran and Alice & Bob's estimator) at a shared accuracy target

gaps.gap: Hardware demonstrations run far below the 100-1,000 logical-qubit target regime
gaps.why_hard: No platform yet sustains that many logical qubits at 1e6-1e9 operation depth
gaps.entry_point: Run early-FT algorithms (QCELS/QET-U) on the largest available logical-qubit testbeds to extrapolate scaling before full fault tolerance arrives

problems.note: Several 2025-2026 advantage claims were qualified or partly matched by classical methods within weeks, so this evidence base is contested and moving fast.
problems.name: Useful early-FT instances

doe.pullWhy: Applicants must name a demonstrator problem; the First-generation tier is a full scientific workflow, and DOE's five 2028 science milestones need instances that fit 100 logical qubits.
doe.verifyWhy: Measurable, but the classical baseline keeps moving.
doe.vv: Quantum versus best-classical cost at matched accuracy; agreement with experiment.

problems.title: Cross-architecture, verifiable fault-tolerant resource estimation
problems.one_liner: Make fault-tolerant resource estimates comparable and trustworthy across superconducting, neutral-atom, ion, and photonic hardware, with shared formats and validated assumptions.
problems.statement: Every fault-tolerant hardware track (superconducting surface/qLDPC codes, neutral atoms with transversal gates, trapped ions, photonics) now has at least one resource-estimation tool, but each uses its own noise model, cost model, and output format, so published numbers cannot be compared or audited across tools. Solving this means building shared exchange formats and assumption registries so two independent tools can consume the same algorithm description; propagating uncertainty so an estimate carries error bars, not a single number; validating cost models against detailed circuit-level simulation or real hardware; and automating the pipeline, including agentic tools, so estimates can be produced and re-checked quickly as compilation improves. 'Solved' means a practitioner can run the same target algorithm through independently maintained estimators for at least two hardware families and get numbers that differ only for genuine physical reasons, with a documented, reproducible reason for any remaining gap, ideally checked by an independent verification process such as DARPA's.

anchors.item: Starling: 200 logical qubits, 1e8 gates - first large-scale fault-tolerant computer
anchors.dependency: Sets the qubit/gate-count regime any credible cross-architecture estimate must eventually target

anchors.item: Grand Challenge of Quantum Applications names compilation/resource-estimation as under-resourced
anchors.dependency: Names cross-architecture resource estimation as a required, currently under-built stage

anchors.item: Gidney RSA-2048 estimate: under 1,000,000 noisy qubits, under 1 week (from 20,000,000/8h in 2019)
anchors.dependency: Shows how fast a single architecture's own resource estimate can move, motivating shared, version-tracked baselines

anchors.item: Libra (2028, >256 logical qubits, ~1e-6) and gigaquop (2028-29, >1,000 logical, ~1e-9) systems
anchors.dependency: Gives concrete target logical-error-rate numbers any neutral-atom estimator must be validated against

criteria_why.C1: Assumption registries are partly engineering, but proving cross-architecture cost equivalence needs new theory
criteria_why.C2: Physical qubit count, runtime, and error rate for a fixed algorithm and accuracy are directly computable and comparable
criteria_why.C3: Once a shared format exists, any group can plug in a new architecture model or algorithm
criteria_why.C4: Each tool (Azure QRE, Qualtran, BenchQ, RRE, company estimators) uses its own assumptions and output format today
criteria_why.C5: Splits naturally into per-architecture models, shared formats, uncertainty quantification, and cross-validation
criteria_why.C6: Deriving apples-to-apples cost models across very different error-correction schemes is technically hard

problems.access_note: Estimators themselves run on classical computers; validation increasingly uses cloud hardware (IBM, Quantinuum) and lab-scale QEC memory experiments

metrics.name: Physical-to-logical qubit overhead
metrics.def: Physical qubits required per logical qubit at a stated logical error rate, for a fixed code family
metrics.sota: IBM's bicycle-code family: 288 physical qubits sustain 12 logical qubits (24x) for ~1e6 syndrome cycles at 0.8% threshold, vs. an estimated ~3,000 physical qubits for an equivalent surface-code memory (Bravyi et al., Nature 627, 2024)

metrics.name: Cross-tool estimate spread for the same target
metrics.def: Ratio between the highest and lowest published physical-resource estimate (qubits x time) for the same target algorithm and accuracy, across independent tools or architectures
metrics.sota: Alice & Bob's cat-qubit estimator reports ~27x fewer physical qubits than a transmon-plus-surface-code baseline for equivalent FeMoco/P450 runtime (2023-2025 estimator); no single study yet reconciles 3+ tools on one shared target

metrics.name: Estimate shrinkage under improved compilation
metrics.def: How much a published resource estimate for the same target problem shrinks after a compilation or algorithmic improvement, tracked across successive papers
metrics.sota: RSA-2048 factoring: 20,000,000 noisy qubits / 8 hours (2019) to under 1,000,000 noisy qubits / under 1 week (Gidney, 2025), a >20x physical-qubit reduction via yoked surface codes and magic-state cultivation

stages.name: Per-tool infrastructure
stages.goal: Each architecture or vendor has at least one working resource estimator
stages.exit: Four or more independently maintained tools exist covering at least three hardware families
stages.note: Azure QRE, Qualtran, BenchQ, RRE, and Alice & Bob's cat-qubit estimator already span superconducting, ion-trap-adjacent, and cat-qubit targets

stages.name: Per-architecture validated cost models
stages.goal: Each tool's cost model is checked against a real experiment or detailed circuit-level simulation for its own architecture
stages.exit: At least one published validation of an estimator against hardware or simulation exists per architecture family
stages.note: IBM's bicycle-code memory experiment validates one qLDPC cost model against real hardware; most other tools are validated only in simulation

stages.name: Shared exchange format and assumption registry
stages.goal: A common, tool-agnostic format lets two different estimators consume the same algorithm description and assumption set
stages.exit: Two or more independent tools demonstrably read or write the same shared format on a shared benchmark
stages.note: PsiQuantum has proposed a shared exchange format (QREF); BenchQ already interoperates with Azure QRE, showing early cross-tool integration

stages.name: Cross-tool, cross-architecture comparison studies
stages.goal: The same target algorithm is estimated independently by two or more tools for two or more hardware families, with results reconciled
stages.exit: A published study reports and explains the size of the gap between at least two independent estimates for one shared target
stages.note: Individual architecture estimates exist for shared targets (e.g. FeMoco under cat qubits vs. earlier surface-code figures; RSA-2048 across successive Google estimates) but head-to-head reconciled comparisons across three or more tools remain rare

stages.name: Independent verification and validation at program scale
stages.goal: A neutral third party audits vendor resource-estimate claims against a common standard
stages.exit: At least one completed independent audit report is published for a named claim
stages.note: DARPA's QBI has proposed an IV&V process, but its Stage A (due Nov 30 2026) and IV&V milestone (due Dec 30 2026) have not yet produced a completed public audit

stages.name: General cross-architecture theory
stages.goal: A predictive theory converts any algorithm plus any architecture's physical parameters into a resource estimate without a bespoke tool
stages.exit: A single formalism reproduces at least three existing tools' published numbers within a stated uncertainty band
stages.note: Beverland et al. (2022) offers the closest general framework, but it targets generic/superconducting qubits, not a fully cross-architecture theory

IBM.headline: Bicycle-code overheads from simulation; no public estimator
IBM.summary: IBM's bicycle-code family reaches a ~0.8% circuit-level threshold and, in simulation, keeps 12 logical qubits for nearly one million syndrome cycles with 288 physical qubits, versus an estimated ~3,000 for a comparable surface-code memory (Bravyi et al., Nature 2024). IBM has not released a third-party-usable estimator comparable to Qualtran or the Azure Quantum Resource Estimator; its figures live in its own code and roadmap papers.

Google.headline: Open-sources Qualtran, a general algorithm-costing library
Google.summary: Google Quantum AI's Qualtran (Harrigan et al., 2024) is an open-source library for representing and analyzing quantum algorithms, generating circuit diagrams, and estimating physical costs (wall-clock time, physical qubits) under a stated surface-code architecture, covering Hamiltonian simulation, chemistry, and cryptography workloads. Its cost model is currently surface-code-specific rather than covering neutral-atom or ion-trap hardware, and Google separately names resource estimation as an under-resourced stage in its own Grand Challenge framework.

QuEra.headline: Harvard/QuEra-affiliated theory gives neutral-atom resource counts; no packaged tool yet
QuEra.summary: QuEra's June 2026 roadmap commits to auditable numbers - a >256-logical-qubit 'Libra' system at about 1e-6 logical error by 2028, and a >1,000-logical-qubit 'gigaquop' system at about 1e-9 by 2028-2029 - and its FTQC Founders Circle (with the BB-STAR co-design case study) invites outside groups to stress-test these assumptions. As of September 2026 QuEra has not published its own open resource-estimation tool comparable to Qualtran, Azure QRE, or BenchQ. A 2023 Harvard/MIT theory paper (Xu, Bonilla Ataides, Pattison, Bluvstein, Lukin, Jiang, Zhou et al.) derives constant-overhead fault-tolerant resource counts for qLDPC codes on reconfigurable neutral-atom arrays, needing under 100,000 physical qubits for algorithms with thousands of logical qubits, though this remains a theoretical estimate rather than a packaged, third-party-usable tool.

IonQ.headline: Fully compiled end-to-end estimates for IonQ's architecture; not comparable across hardware.
IonQ.summary: IonQ's September 2026 secp256k1 estimate is presented as the first fully compiled end-to-end resource estimate: it accounts for arithmetic optimization, logical instruction set, scheduling, ion routing and transport, error-correction design and physical allocation, giving 19,397 physical qubits, 1,457 logical qubits and 25.7 days per attempt. The Walking Cat paper gives similar estimates for Heisenberg simulation and Shor. Both use IonQ's own noise and timing assumptions; no common cost model across hardware platforms is published.
IonQ.gateWhy: Comparable estimates are needed to justify the 100-logical-qubit First-generation plan; IonQ has published estimates only for its own platform.

Community.headline: Most active layer: independent tools, DARPA-funded estimators, modular-hardware studies
Community.summary: Community and industry groups supply most of the field's tooling: Microsoft's Azure Quantum Resource Estimator (Beverland et al. 2022; van Dam, Mykhailova & Soeken 2023) set the template later tools follow; Zapata's DARPA-funded BenchQ and Rigetti's RRE add graph-state and measurement-based-computing cost models; Alice & Bob publish cat-qubit estimates (about 99,000 qubits for FeMoco, about 27x fewer than a transmon-plus-surface-code baseline); Kan & Symons (IBM) resource-optimize Fermi-Hubbard-family circuits; and Saadatmand et al. (2024) model costs for million-qubit modular superconducting systems. DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative is separately building an independent-verification process, with first milestones due late 2026.

overall.headline: Many tools, no shared format or completed cross-architecture audit yet
overall.summary: As of September 2026, resource estimation is tool-rich but comparison-poor: Azure QRE, Qualtran, BenchQ, RRE, and company-specific estimators (Alice & Bob, IBM's own bicycle-code analysis) each cover their own hardware assumptions, and only IBM's qLDPC memory result has been checked against real hardware at meaningful scale. No published study reconciles three or more tools on one shared target algorithm, and DARPA's QBI - the most concrete push toward independent verification - has its first formal milestones (Stage A, IV&V) due only in late 2026, so a genuinely cross-architecture, audited resource-estimation practice does not yet exist.

gaps.gap: No shared exchange format is in general use across tools
gaps.why_hard: Each tool encodes assumptions (noise model, code family, compilation strategy) differently, and translating between them can silently change the answer
gaps.entry_point: Publish one small benchmark circuit's resource estimate from two tools (e.g. Qualtran and BenchQ) side by side, documenting every assumption that differs

gaps.gap: Almost no estimates are validated against real hardware at scale
gaps.why_hard: Current hardware does not yet run at the logical-qubit counts the estimates target, so validation is limited to small subsystems
gaps.entry_point: Use IBM's bicycle-code memory result (288 physical/12 logical qubits, 0.8% threshold) as a validation anchor and check whether other tools' cost models reproduce it

gaps.gap: IV&V processes exist on paper but have not produced a public audit
gaps.why_hard: DARPA QBI's Stage A and IV&V milestones are still upcoming (due Nov-Dec 2026), so there is no precedent for what a completed independent audit looks like
gaps.entry_point: Track DARPA QBI's first Stage A submissions (due Nov 30, 2026) as the first real test case for an external audit methodology

problems.note: Tools target different hardware assumptions, so the open problem is comparability, not picking a winner. Architecture-specific savings should not be read as one platform being better.
problems.name: Comparable resource estimates

doe.pullWhy: The RFA encourages every applicant to convert its roadmap to logical qubits and hard operations, and asks for hard and easy operation counts and wall-clock time for a demonstrator.
doe.vv: Spread between tools for the same target; error between estimate and measurement.

problems.title: Logical-Level Benchmarking and Reporting Standards
problems.one_liner: Agreeing on reproducible metrics and protocols so logical-qubit and operation-budget claims across companies can be independently checked, not just self-reported.
problems.statement: Every 2026 roadmap reports logical performance differently. Google publishes logical error per cycle and the error-suppression factor Lambda. QuEra replaced logical-qubit counts with operation budgets: megaquop for Libra by 2028, meaning more than 256 logical qubits at a 1e-6 error rate, and gigaquop for 2028 to 2029, more than 1,000 at 1e-9. IBM counts 100 million quantum gates on 200 logical qubits for Starling by 2029. Without shared definitions of what counts as a logical qubit, how post-selection and leakage or loss are treated, and what a logical operation means across different codes and platforms, these numbers cannot be compared or independently checked. The problem is to define reproducible, community-agreed protocols, including logical randomized benchmarking, logical-circuit and volumetric benchmarks, and explicit treatment of post-selection and leakage, plus institutional mechanisms such as DARPA's QBI, QED-C, IEEE, NIST, and open platforms like Metriq that verify vendor claims against them. A solved version produces a published benchmark suite and reporting standard that a third party can run on any platform, onto which most current roadmap claims can be mapped.

anchors.item: Reports logical error per cycle and the error-suppression factor Lambda as primary metrics; d=7 gives 7.72e-4 logical error/cycle
anchors.dependency: No cross-vendor standard yet specifies exactly how Lambda should be measured/reported

anchors.item: Replaced logical-qubit counts with operation budgets: 'megaquop' Libra 2028 (>256 logical qubits at 1e-6), 'gigaquop' 2028-2029 (>1,000 at 1e-9)
anchors.dependency: No independent protocol yet verifies operation-budget claims the way logical RB verifies error rates

anchors.item: Starling target: 100 million quantum gates on 200 logical qubits
anchors.dependency: No published protocol defines how a gate-count-on-logical-qubits claim should be independently measured or certified

anchors.item: DARPA Quantum Benchmarking Initiative (QBI): 3-stage independent verification of utility-scale claims; QuEra selected for Stage B (Nov 2025)
anchors.dependency: QBI's verification protocol could become the closest thing to a cross-vendor logical-benchmarking standard

criteria_why.C1: Defining protocols robust to post-selection and leakage across different codes is open research, not routine engineering.
criteria_why.C2: Metrics such as logical error per cycle exist, but no agreed protocol yet makes cross-platform numbers directly comparable.
criteria_why.C3: Once a suite exists, any group with cloud or lab access can run and report results, as Metriq shows.
criteria_why.C4: No single agreed standard exists: Google, QuEra, and IBM each report performance in a different currency today.
criteria_why.C5: Naturally stages from single-metric definitions to full suites to institutional certification via DARPA's QBI and IEEE.
criteria_why.C6: Proving a benchmark is unbiased under post-selection and leakage for arbitrary codes is technically hard, not routine.

problems.access_note: Many application-level benchmarks run on public cloud QPUs; full logical-level RB needs QEC-capable hardware access.

metrics.name: Logical error rate per cycle
metrics.def: Probability of a logical error per QEC cycle, measured via repeated syndrome-extraction rounds.
metrics.sota: 7.72e-4 per cycle at distance 7 (Google, Nature, July 2026)

metrics.name: Lambda (error-suppression factor)
metrics.def: Ratio of logical error improvement per code-distance increase (d to d+2); Lambda greater than 1 indicates below-threshold scaling.
metrics.sota: Reported by Google as a primary below-threshold metric across its 2023-2026 surface-code series

metrics.name: Operation budget (megaquop/gigaquop)
metrics.def: Total number of reliable logical operations available at a stated logical error rate, replacing raw qubit counts.
metrics.sota: QuEra's Libra target: more than 256 logical qubits at 1e-6 by 2028 (megaquop); more than 1,000 at 1e-9 by 2028-2029 (gigaquop)

metrics.name: Logical randomized benchmarking fidelity
metrics.def: An RB decay curve applied at the logical level to estimate an average logical error rate without assuming a noise model.
metrics.sota: Introduced by Combes et al. in 2017; not yet a required cross-vendor report

infra.name: Metriq
infra.what: Community-run platform executing and publishing reproducible cross-vendor benchmark results

infra.name: QED-C application-oriented benchmark suite
infra.what: Open-source, vendor-neutral benchmark suite run across multiple cloud QPUs

infra.name: Volumetric / mirror-circuit benchmark toolkit
infra.what: Sandia framework (pyGSTi-adjacent) for structured-circuit capability benchmarking

infra.name: IEEE P7131 working group
infra.what: Standards process for quantum computing performance metrics and benchmarking

stages.name: Metric definitions and single-platform benchmarks
stages.goal: Define logical error rate, Lambda, and logical RB as measurable, well-specified quantities.
stages.exit: A published, reproducible protocol for at least one logical-level metric with a worked hardware example.
stages.note: Logical RB (2017) and volumetric/mirror-circuit benchmarks (2020-2022) are already established, building on 2017 RB-interpretation work.

stages.name: Cross-platform application-oriented suites
stages.goal: Build benchmark suites usable across vendors and hardware, not tied to one company's stack.
stages.exit: A suite runs unmodified on three or more independent hardware backends with published results.
stages.note: The QED-C suite and Metriq already run across multiple vendors' cloud hardware.

stages.name: Logical-level reporting in practice: post-selection and leakage treatment
stages.goal: Get vendors to report logical-level numbers, including how post-selection and leakage were handled.
stages.exit: A widely used reporting convention distinguishes post-selected from unconditional logical error rates for any claim.
stages.note: Google reports unconditional logical error/Lambda; a 2024 Quantinuum/Microsoft 'no errors' claim drew public scrutiny over post-selection.

stages.name: Independent / third-party verification programs
stages.goal: Move beyond self-reported vendor numbers to third-party or government verification.
stages.exit: At least one company's roadmap claim is independently verified end-to-end under a program such as DARPA's QBI.
stages.note: DARPA's QBI Stage B is underway (QuEra, Nov 2025); no public Stage C verification has completed yet.

stages.name: Formal cross-vendor reporting standard
stages.goal: Reach a ratified standard, such as IEEE P7131, that vendors are expected to report against.
stages.exit: IEEE P7131 or an equivalent body publishes a ratified standard cited by two or more hardware vendors' public reporting.
stages.note: The IEEE P7131 working group is active but has not yet published a ratified standard as of September 2026.

IBM.headline: Announced a 2029 gate-count target with no public verification protocol yet.
IBM.summary: IBM's roadmap states that Starling, planned for 2029, will run 100 million quantum gates on 200 logical qubits, a concrete operation-budget-style target. IBM has not published an accompanying third-party-checkable benchmarking protocol for this number, and it currently functions as a roadmap projection rather than a measured, externally verified result.

Google.headline: Most detailed public logical-level reporting among the three companies.
Google.summary: Google has reported logical error per cycle and the error-suppression factor Lambda across its 2023-2026 surface-code papers, from an initial demonstration of error suppression scaling with code distance (Nature, 2023) to 7.72e-4 logical error per cycle at distance 7 with an RL-tuned calibration loop (Nature, July 2026). This is the most quantitatively specific, hardware-measured logical metric among the three companies, though self-reported using Google's own definitions rather than a cross-vendor standard.

QuEra.headline: Redefined reporting around operation budgets instead of logical-qubit counts.
QuEra.summary: QuEra's June 2026 roadmap replaced logical-qubit-count claims with operation-budget targets: megaquop (Libra, 2028: more than 256 logical qubits at 1e-6 error) and gigaquop (2028-2029: more than 1,000 at 1e-9). This is a genuine shift away from raw qubit counts, but remains a self-defined metric with no independent verification yet published; QuEra's Stage B participation in DARPA's QBI (November 2025) is the closest thing to third-party scrutiny in progress.

IonQ.headline: Physical-level #AQ benchmark plus one post-selected logical breakeven comparison; no verification protocol.
IonQ.summary: IonQ's long-running benchmark is #AQ (algorithmic qubits), a physical-level application-suite metric: a 2023 paper reports #AQ 29 on a modified QED-C suite for Forte, and IonQ announced #AQ 64 on Tempo in September 2025, saying it will report logical metrics separately. At the logical level, the 2026 breakeven experiment compares fitted logical lifetimes with a measured 3.84 s physical-qubit lifetime, and a later paper reanalyzes the data with soft decoding. Both are IonQ-run and post-selected; no protocol for independent logical-level verification is published.
IonQ.gateWhy: A 10-logical-qubit Prototype claim needs a reproducible logical-level metric, which IonQ's 2026 logical-qubit step also implies.

Community.headline: Supplies the shared metrics and platforms vendor claims get checked against.
Community.summary: Logical randomized benchmarking (Combes et al., 2017) and volumetric/mirror-circuit benchmarks (Proctor et al., Sandia, 2020/2022) remain the main vendor-independent assessment tools, building on earlier work clarifying what standard randomized benchmarking actually measures (Proctor et al., 2017). QED-C's application-oriented benchmark suite (Lubinski et al., 2021) and the Unitary Foundation's Metriq platform provide running, cross-vendor infrastructure. IEEE's P7131 working group and DARPA's QBI are the two active institutional efforts turning these into enforceable standards, but neither has yet produced a ratified, widely adopted logical-level standard as of September 2026.

overall.headline: Metrics exist per vendor; a shared, verified standard does not yet.
overall.summary: By 2026 each roadmap leader reports logical performance differently: Google via logical error per cycle and Lambda, QuEra via operation budgets (megaquop/gigaquop), and IBM via a 2029 gate-count target, while a widely covered 2024 Quantinuum/Microsoft 'no errors' logical-qubit claim drew scrutiny over post-selection. Academic tools (logical randomized benchmarking, volumetric benchmarks) and community infrastructure (QED-C, Metriq) supply pieces a shared standard would need. DARPA's QBI (QuEra in Stage B, November 2025) and IEEE P7131 are the active institutional attempts at cross-vendor verification, but neither has published a ratified standard vendors are held to, so 2026-era roadmap numbers remain self-reported.

gaps.gap: No agreed treatment of post-selection or leakage in reported logical error rates
gaps.why_hard: Excluding failed shots inflates apparent fidelity, and there is no consensus threshold for how much post-selection a claim may use.
gaps.entry_point: Publish a short benchmark requiring both post-selected and unconditional logical error rates side by side for any claim.

gaps.gap: Operation-budget metrics like megaquop and gigaquop have no independent verification protocol
gaps.why_hard: They aggregate many circuit types into one number, so no single randomized-benchmarking-style experiment can check them directly.
gaps.entry_point: Define a minimal operation-budget audit: a fixed circuit family whose logical success rate a third party can run and compare to the claimed budget.

gaps.gap: IEEE P7131 and DARPA's QBI have not yet published a ratified cross-vendor standard
gaps.why_hard: Standards bodies move slowly relative to roadmap pace, and vendors have incentives to keep their own self-defined metrics.
gaps.entry_point: Community groups such as Metriq and QED-C can pre-empt slow standards bodies by publishing a de facto suite vendors adopt voluntarily.

problems.note: IBM's and QuEra's headline numbers are 2028-2029 targets, not measurements. Google publishes measured logical error per cycle with data.
problems.name: Logical-level benchmarks

doe.pullWhy: DOE will 'agree on an objective methodology' with each awardee as part of the first milestone, and every tier is judged with these benchmarks.
doe.vv: Hard operations completed reliably; logical error per operation; logical circuit width and depth.

problems.title: Formal verification of fault-tolerant stacks
problems.one_liner: Machine-checked guarantees for codes, syndrome circuits, decoders, compilers, and end-to-end algorithms, scaling to roadmap-size fault-tolerant systems.
problems.statement: Fault-tolerant quantum stacks stack many layers that must each be correct: the error-correcting code itself (does it have the claimed distance?), the syndrome-extraction circuit (does it preserve fault distance despite its own faults?), the decoder (does it always output a valid, likely correction?), the logical compiler (does it preserve the algorithm's semantics through lattice surgery, transversal gates, or Pauli-based scheduling?), and the end-to-end algorithm (does the whole pipeline compute what it claims?). Today these are verified separately, by ad hoc testing or bespoke proofs, with no shared machine-checked framework connecting them, and no verification effort has been demonstrated near the several-hundred-logical-qubit, ~1e8-gate scale the 2026-2029 roadmaps target. 'Solved' means machine-checked (Coq/Rocq/Lean-style) proof libraries exist for each layer, compose so a proof about one layer's guarantees can be reused when checking the next, and have been exercised on at least one fault-tolerant architecture close to roadmap scale, not just toy circuits.

anchors.item: Bicycle-code logical instruction set ('Tour de gross'); Starling 2029 target (200 logical qubits, 1e8 gates)
anchors.dependency: A verified compiler/decoder is needed before roadmap-scale runs on this ISA can be trusted as correct rather than merely tested.

anchors.item: Milestone 4 lattice surgery/color-code transversal gates; 86.5-90.7% fidelity teleportation demo
anchors.dependency: Verified syndrome circuits/decoders would let claimed fidelities be attributed to the code rather than to post-selection or tuning.

anchors.item: Libra (2028): >256 logical qubits at 1e-6 error, 'High-Rate QEC'; Harvard/QuEra AFT claims O(1) syndrome rounds per logical layer
anchors.dependency: Distance/fault-distance certificates and decoder-soundness proofs are needed to trust the claimed error rate at this scale.

criteria_why.C1: Composable machine-checked proofs spanning codes, circuits, decoders and compilers is original formal-methods + QEC research.
criteria_why.C2: Feedback is crisp: the proof checker accepts or rejects, and verification time/coverage are directly measurable.
criteria_why.C3: Once a framework exists, formal-methods groups steadily extend it to new codes/circuits, as the 2021-2026 paper cadence shows.
criteria_why.C4: No system found spans distance-certificate, circuit, decoder, compiler and algorithm proofs together today.
criteria_why.C5: Cleanly decomposes by stack layer (code, circuit, decoder, compiler, algorithm) and by scale.
criteria_why.C6: General distance certification and decoder-soundness proofs are genuinely hard; existing proofs stay narrow in scope.

problems.access_note: Verification is proof-assistant/software work; any empirical fault-distance search needs classical simulation, not hardware.

metrics.name: Machine-checked proof (pass/fail)
metrics.def: Whether a Coq/Rocq/Lean proof script type-checks against the stated theorem, per verification run.
metrics.sota: Demonstrated for circuit-optimizer correctness (2021) and full Shor's-algorithm correctness (2023); not yet for an FT-encoded, decoder-including pipeline.

metrics.name: Verified-program size (T-gate / qubit count reached)
metrics.def: Largest Clifford+T program size (T-gate count, qubit count) a verification technique has been demonstrated on.
metrics.sota: 7-qubit Steane encoder and small Toffoli/graph-state circuits verified with low proof overhead (Cho & Rand, VMCAI 2026); roadmap scale not yet attempted.

metrics.name: Verification/proof-checking wall-clock time
metrics.def: CPU time for the proof assistant (or a SAT/SMT solver, for distance-certificate-style checks) to check a given property.
metrics.sota: Not reported at roadmap scale in the literature surveyed; existing tools report times only for small/medium circuits.

infra.name: SQIR / VOQC
infra.what: Coq-formalized small quantum IR plus a verified circuit optimizer, with a Python wrapper.

infra.name: pyvoqc
infra.what: Python wrapper around the VOQC verified quantum-circuit optimizer.

stages.name: Formal semantics and base proof tooling
stages.goal: Machine-checked language semantics for (unencoded) quantum circuits/IRs
stages.exit: A proof-assistant-formalized circuit/IR semantics used by >=2 independent verification papers
stages.note: SQIR and CoqQ provide independently-developed foundational semantics reused by later work.

stages.name: Verified compiler passes / optimizers on unencoded circuits
stages.goal: Prove individual circuit-rewrite/optimization passes preserve semantics
stages.exit: A push-button-verified pass suite covering a real compiler's optimizations
stages.note: Demonstrated for Qiskit-style passes (Giallar, 2022) and a dedicated verified optimizer (VOQC, 2021).

stages.name: Verified small end-to-end algorithms
stages.goal: Full-program correctness proofs for specific complete algorithms
stages.exit: A complete algorithm proved correct end-to-end including classical pre/post-processing
stages.note: Achieved once, for Shor's factorization (PNAS 2023); not yet repeated for other algorithms or FT-encoded versions.

stages.name: Verified FT-compilation properties
stages.goal: Prove compiler/scheduler outputs respect FT-specific constraints (connectivity, magic-state usage, few-T-gate circuits)
stages.exit: A type system or proof technique verifying a real lattice-surgery/FT compiler's output against connectivity or resource constraints
stages.note: APLAS 2024/2025 verifies lattice-surgery connectivity; VMCAI 2026 verifies small Clifford+T/Steane-code circuits.

stages.name: Verified codes, syndrome circuits and decoders at moderate scale
stages.goal: Machine-checked distance certificates for codes/circuits and correctness/soundness proofs for decoders
stages.exit: A proof or SAT/MILP-certified distance bound for a qLDPC/bicycle code plus a verified decoder-soundness result, at tens-to-hundreds of logical qubits
stages.note: No verified decoder or machine-checked qLDPC distance certificate has been published; a known gap (see gaps).

stages.name: Composed, roadmap-scale end-to-end verified FT stack
stages.goal: Single machine-checked framework composing code+circuit+decoder+compiler+algorithm proofs at Starling/Libra scale
stages.exit: A published proof chain covering all five layers for one real algorithm at >=100 logical qubits
stages.note: Not attempted; the field is still building single-layer proofs.

IBM.headline: No IBM-led verification work found; Qiskit itself is a third-party verification target.
IBM.summary: No IBM-authored formal-verification publication targeting its own fault-tolerant stack was found. IBM's Qiskit compiler is, however, the subject of independent academic verification (Giallar, PLDI 2022), and OpenQASM's wide adoption makes IBM's stack a natural future target for the layer-by-layer verification work described above. No evidence was found of IBM applying formal methods to its bicycle-code ('Tour de gross') logical instruction set itself.

Google.headline: No Google-authored formal-verification publication targeting its FT stack was found.
Google.summary: No Google-authored or Google-targeted formal-verification paper was identified in this review. Google's public contributions in this space (e.g. Qualtran) are resource-estimation and algorithm-expression tools, not correctness-verification tools, and no published proof was found covering Google's color-code lattice-surgery or transversal-gate implementations.

QuEra.headline: No QuEra-authored formal-verification publication targeting its FT stack was found.
QuEra.summary: No QuEra-authored or QuEra-targeted formal-verification paper was identified in this review. QuEra's Bloqade compiler and the Harvard/QuEra algorithmic-fault-tolerance result are simulation- and hardware-validated, not machine-proof-verified; no published distance certificate, verified decoder, or verified compiler pass was found for QuEra's neutral-atom stack.

IonQ.headline: No public IonQ work on machine-checked guarantees for codes, decoders or compilers.
IonQ.summary: No IonQ work on formal verification of error-correcting codes, syndrome circuits, decoders or compilers has been published. IonQ's decoder, code and compiler papers rely on numerical simulation and, for the 2026 breakeven experiment, hardware data; none reports a proof-assistant or other machine-checked guarantee, so the problem is open on IonQ's side.
IonQ.gateWhy: IonQ's roadmap does not include verified-stack milestones.

Community.headline: Academic PL/formal-methods groups drive nearly all progress, one layer at a time.
Community.summary: Progress is almost entirely academic: a University of Maryland/Chicago line (Hietala, Rand, Hicks, Peng) produced the verified SQIR/VOQC optimizer (2021) and the first certified end-to-end Shor's algorithm (2023), and continues with a 2026 few-T-gate verifier (Cho & Rand); Columbia's team built Giallar (2022) to verify Qiskit's own compiler passes; a CoqQ line (2023) gives foundational quantum-Hoare-style verification; and a Kyoto University/NTT team (2024/2025) built the first type system verifying lattice-surgery connectivity. No cross-institution effort yet composes these into one multi-layer proof.

overall.headline: Verification proceeds one stack layer at a time; no cross-layer or roadmap-scale proof exists yet.
overall.summary: Formal-methods groups have verified individual layers of the fault-tolerant stack -- a circuit optimizer (VOQC, 2021), a real compiler's passes (Giallar, 2022), a complete algorithm's correctness (certified Shor, 2023), a foundational quantum program logic (CoqQ, 2023), lattice-surgery connectivity typing (APLAS 2024/2025), and small Clifford+T circuits with few T gates (VMCAI 2026) -- but no company has published a formally verified compiler, decoder, or code targeting its own 2026-2029 roadmap hardware. IBM's, Google's and QuEra's roadmap claims currently rest on testing and simulation rather than machine-checked proof.

gaps.gap: No machine-checked distance certificate for a roadmap-scale qLDPC/bicycle code.
gaps.why_hard: General qLDPC minimum-distance computation is believed hard in general, and a proof-assistant-checked bound needs both an efficient certificate algorithm and a formalized correctness proof of it.
gaps.entry_point: Formalize an existing SAT/MILP or LP-relaxation distance-lower-bound method inside a proof assistant so its output becomes a checked certificate rather than a trusted external computation.

gaps.gap: No verified decoder (soundness/completeness proof) has been demonstrated.
gaps.why_hard: Practical decoders (MWPM, BP+OSD, neural) are complex numerical/graph algorithms; proving they never output an invalid or systematically wrong correction requires reasoning beyond discrete program semantics.
gaps.entry_point: Start with a machine-checked correctness proof for the simplest exact decoder (lookup-table decoding for a small surface-code patch) and grow the code distance incrementally.

gaps.gap: Verification results stop at small circuits/codes; nothing has scaled toward the ~200-logical-qubit / 1e8-gate roadmap targets.
gaps.why_hard: Proof-assistant effort tends to grow faster than program size, and no compositional theory yet lets a large FT circuit's proof be assembled from small, reusable verified pieces.
gaps.entry_point: Extend the few-T-gate verifier (Cho & Rand, VMCAI 2026) with a compositional proof rule for concatenating verified sub-circuits, then test it on a moderate (dozens of logical qubits) FT circuit.

problems.note: Verification proceeds one layer of the stack at a time; none of the three companies has published formal verification of its own fault-tolerant stack.
problems.name: Verified fault-tolerant stacks

doe.pullWhy: First-generation runs can be checked against classical results; production runs at 10⁷ hard operations cannot, so on all four roadmaps trust must eventually come from verified software and decoders.
doe.verifyWhy: Pass/fail proofs and verified-program size are computable, but they are not V&V hardware quantities.
doe.vv: Machine-checked components and the largest verified program.
