IBM.summary: IBM's roadmap runs two parallel tracks: an 'Advantage-scale' Nighthawk line (120 qubits; two-qubit gate budgets rising 5,000→7,500→10,000→15,000 across 2025-2028) and a fault-tolerant qLDPC track (Loon 2025 → Kookaburra 2026 → Cockatoo 2027 → Starling 2029: 200 logical qubits/100M gates at a new Poughkeepsie, NY data center → Blue Jay 2033+: 2,000 logical qubits/1B gates). The architecture rests on bivariate-bicycle ('gross') qLDPC codes reaching surface-code-level thresholds (~0.8%) with roughly 10x fewer physical qubits, decoded by the Relay-BP algorithm, which IBM and AMD demonstrated on off-the-shelf FPGAs in late 2025. Loon and Nighthawk were delivered by November 2025, Loon achieving under-480-nanosecond real-time decoding about a year ahead of schedule. Through 2026, IBM committed over $10 billion over five years, finalized a CHIPS-Act-backed 'Anderon' 300mm quantum foundry, partnered with Cisco on post-2029 quantum networking, and had CEO Arvind Krishna declare at Think 2026 that quantum advantage would arrive 'within the year.' In July 2026, IBM and academic/industry partners posted three candidate quantum-advantage papers; independent physicists call them credible but not fully adjudicated, and a classical rebuttal preprint has since challenged at least one claim. No public confirmation of a delivered 2026 Kookaburra module was found as of this writing; an independent blogger has also sharply disputed IBM's fault-tolerance timeline as premature.

Google.summary: Google Quantum AI's public roadmap is milestone-based, not year-based. Six milestones raise physical-qubit scale roughly tenfold per step (54, ~10^2, 10^3, 10^4, 10^5, 10^6) while pushing logical error from ~1e-2 (Milestone 2) to 1e-6 (Milestones 3-5) and 1e-13 (Milestone 6). Only Milestone 1 (beyond-classical, 2019) and Milestone 2 (QEC prototype, 2023) carry dates. The 105-qubit Willow chip (Dec 2024) showed below-threshold surface-code memory (distance 7, Lambda 2.14, 0.143% error per cycle) with real-time decoding at distance 5. Google describes this as progress 'towards Milestone 3', not Milestone 3 itself. Since then Google has published building blocks for later milestones: color codes with transversal Clifford gates and lattice-surgery teleportation, dynamic surface codes, magic state cultivation on hardware (fidelity 0.9999 with 8% of attempts kept), the AlphaQubit 2 decoder, and in-loop reinforcement-learning calibration that brought distance-7 error down to 7.72e-4 per cycle (Nature, Jul 2026). It also reported 'verifiable quantum advantage' with Quantum Echoes (Oct 2025). As of Sept 2026, Google has not claimed Milestone 3 (1e-6) or Milestone 4 (logical gate), and no processor after Willow is public. Three strategic updates came in March 2026: neutral atoms were added as a second hardware modality, Google set 2029 as its own post-quantum cryptography migration deadline, and it published a 256-bit elliptic-curve attack estimate below 500,000 physical qubits. Google's only dated forward statements are qualitative: real-world applications 'within five years' (Feb 2025) and commercially relevant superconducting computers 'by the end of this decade' (Mar 2026).

changes.change: Baseline goal: "Within the decade", a useful, error-corrected quantum computer built from 1,000,000 physical qubits.
Milestone 2 achieved (Lambda about 1.04). Target restated as logical error of 1e-6 per cycle or lower, e.g. Lambda 4 at distance 17 (577 qubits).
Willow shows below-threshold QEC. Google names the field's next challenge: a first 'useful, beyond-classical' computation on Willow-generation chips.
Neven sets a public five-year horizon for real-world quantum-only applications; Julian Kelly echoes 'about five years' in March 2025.
RSA-2048 estimate cut from 20 million to under 1 million noisy qubits (under a week), within Milestone 6's 10^6 scale.
Quantum Echoes adds 'verifiable quantum advantage' to Google's achievements; the long-lived logical qubit (Milestone 3) is restated as the next roadmap milestone.
Atlantic Quantum joins Google to help scale superconducting hardware (integrated cold-stage control electronics).
Application roadmap recast as a five-stage framework; Google says no application has yet reached conclusive real-world advantage (Stage V).
Neutral atoms added as a second modality. Google 'increasingly confident' of commercially relevant superconducting computers 'by the end of this decade'.
Google sets 2029 for its own post-quantum cryptography migration, citing hardware, QEC and factoring-estimate progress.
ECDLP-256 estimate: under 500,000 physical qubits, minutes of runtime; attack circuits withheld and backed by a zero-knowledge proof.
Best published distance-7 error improves to 7.72e-4 per cycle with RL control, about half the 2024 value.
Roadmap page unchanged: six milestones, dates only for Milestones 1-2, no neutral-atom milestones.

assessments.point: Below-threshold scaling is "a very important threshold", but no fault-tolerant two-qubit logical gates near 1e-6 exist yet. The RCS result sits in an unverifiable regime.
Willow's error-correction progress is real. The '10 septillion years' comparison is misleading because the benchmark task has no practical use yet.
Quantum Echoes is verifiable, unlike 2019 RCS, but narrow. Classical shortcuts could emerge, and the experiment needed about one trillion measurements.
2025 progress led him to take 'more seriously' the roadmaps of Google, Quantinuum, QuEra and others 'about where they could be in 2028 or 2029'.
On Google's zero-knowledge-proof ECDLP paper: once others know a smaller circuit exists, they may soon find it. He urges upgrading to quantum-resistant cryptography now.

assessments.who: Scott Aaronson, as reported by PostQuantum (Apr 2026)
assessments.point: Says hardware and QEC experts he trusts believe a fault-tolerant machine able to break deployed cryptosystems 'ought to be possible by around 2029'.
Lower ECDLP resource estimates are not an attack capability. Fault-tolerant architecture, error correction, real-time decoding and control systems remain unbuilt.
Contrasts Google's ~500k-qubit, minutes-long ECDLP estimate with Oratomic's ~26k-qubit neutral-atom estimate that would take about 10 days.
Frames the neutral-atom move as addressing a space-time trade-off: superconducting qubits excel in circuit depth, neutral atoms in qubit count.

open_questions: When will Google claim Milestone 3, and will it report 1e-6 per cycle for a memory only or during logical operations?
Which scheme will deliver Milestone 4 (surface-code lattice surgery, color-code transversal gates, or another), and at what code distance?
What processor follows the 105-qubit Willow, and when will a 10^3 to 10^4-qubit device be disclosed?
Does 'commercially relevant by the end of this decade' mean Milestone 5, Milestone 6, or an intermediate machine?
Will neutral atoms get their own roadmap milestones and dates, or share the existing six?
Can Lambda reach about 4 on larger chips, and will correlated bursts or leakage cap logical error before 1e-13?
How will Google connect and control 10^6 qubits: one cryostat, modular chips, or links between cryostats?
Will AlphaQubit 2-class decoders run closed-loop on hardware at distance 11 or more, with feed-forward for logical gates?
Can magic state cultivation reach about 1e-9 on hardware with an acceptable retention rate?
Which problem instances will Google put forward as its first useful beyond-classical application?
Will the withheld ECDLP circuits be independently reproduced or improved?

QuEra.summary: QuEra's roadmap rests on Harvard/MIT work with reconfigurable rubidium-atom arrays: atoms are shuttled between zones so logical gates can be applied transversally and decoded jointly, and 2025 theory ('algorithmic fault tolerance') argues this needs only O(1) syndrome rounds per logical layer. The January 2024 roadmap promised yearly systems: 10 logical qubits on 256+ atoms (2024), 30 on 3,000+ with magic-state distillation (2025), and 100 on 10,000+ (2026). Laboratory results exceeded the 2024-2025 logical-qubit counts and approached the 2026 one: 48 error-detecting logical qubits (2023); up to 96 distance-4 logical qubits, 2.14x below-threshold surface-code scaling, logical magic-state distillation and 3,000-atom continuous reloading (2025). These relied on small codes, post-selection, or no computation at scale. Shipped hardware stayed at the Gemini class (260 atoms, launched 2025, installed at AIST). The 2026 system has not appeared and is no longer on the roadmap. In June 2026 QuEra replaced qubit-count milestones with operation budgets: Libra, a 'megaquop' machine (>256 logical qubits, 10^-6 logical error, >10,000 atoms) on Amazon Braket in 2028, and a 'gigaquop' successor (>1,000 logical, 10^-9, >20,000 atoms in one core) for initial internal use in 2028-2029. The main open problems are ~99.9% gates at scale, real-time correlated decoding, logic on high-rate qLDPC codes (so far simulated only as memory), and low-overhead magic states.

changes.change: Three-year roadmap: 10 logical/256+ physical qubits with transversal gates (2024), 30/3,000+ with magic-state distillation (2025), 100/10,000+ with deep circuits (2026).
UK NQCC qubit-shuttling and error-correction testbed announced, expected to be operational in early 2025.
AIST contract (JPY 6.5B) for a 2025 on-premises gate-based system next to the ABCI-Q supercomputer.
Alex Keesling moves out of the CEO role; board member Andy Ory named acting CEO (CEO in later releases).
$230M financing (Google, SoftBank Vision Fund 2, Valor); release restates the fault-tolerance goal without year-by-year logical-qubit targets.
First on-premises installation (AIST); QuEra also reports shipping a system to the UK NQCC.
DARPA QBI Stage B selection; QuEra frames its long-range goal as utility-scale computing by 2033.
Year-end review says four Nature papers 'resolved' key scaling risks and promises 'third-generation systems in 2026-2027', not a 2026 100-logical-qubit system.
Ultra-high-rate qLDPC memory simulations (~2 physical qubits per logical) published; later cited in the next-gen 'Ultra-High-Rate QEC' plan.
Roadmap reframed around operation budgets: Libra megaquop (>256 logical, 10^-6) on Braket in 2028; roadmap page lists no 2026 system.
Gigaquop next-gen (>1,000 logical, 10^-9, >20,000 physical in one core) targeted for 2028-2029 internal use; FTQC Founders Circle launched.
HPE collaboration announced as an on-premises HPC path, including potential gigaquop-class deployments.

assessments.point: The 48-logical-qubit IQP demo required post-selecting on no detected errors (~0.1% of runs) and showed no full error-correction cycle, yet was 'plausibly the top' 2023 advance.
'Libra is not a CRQC'; Rydberg two-qubit fidelities of 99.5-99.7% must improve, and real-time qLDPC decoding at 256-logical scale is undemonstrated on any platform.
The 3,000-atom continuous-operation result showed memory and reloading, not computation or QEC at scale; 'several hundred logical qubits' remain a projection.
Algorithmic fault tolerance rests on proofs and simulations, assuming efficient decoders, low-noise magic states, local stochastic noise and tight feed-forward latency.
The '2:1' ratio is a simulated memory result: codes are unbuilt, universal logical gates are missing, and computation overhead will be additional.
Memory-only 2:1 overhead may grow 5-10x for computation; gate error budget nears a ~99.9% physical limit; decoders need microsecond-scale FPGA/ASIC throughput.
No quantum computer yet beats classical alternatives on a commercially relevant problem; 'There is no off-the-shelf path to quantum advantage.'
Neutral-atom operations run 100-1,000x slower than superconducting ones; QuEra argues parallelism and lower error-correction overhead compensate.

open_questions: Will any QuEra system run repeated QEC on more than 10,000 atoms before Libra's 2028 launch, and at what physical error rate?
How will Libra's 10^-6 logical error rate be defined and independently verified: per operation or per round, and without post-selection?
Can correlated decoding keep pace with transversal-gate circuits on 256+ logical qubits without stalling feed-forward?
Do ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes keep their simulated advantage once logical gates, atom loss, idling and movement errors are included?
Which magic-state route (distillation, tricycle codes or STAR injection) will Libra use, and at what space-time cost?
Can two-qubit gate error near 10^-3 be reached uniformly across 10,000-20,000 rubidium atoms?
Will the 'third-generation' continuously operating logical systems promised for 2026-2027 be shown publicly, and are they Libra prototypes?
What wall-clock time per shot will megaquop and gigaquop workloads need at neutral-atom cycle rates?
How does a 20,000-atom single core extend toward the projected 100,000 atoms per chamber, and beyond without interconnects?
What are the operational status and specifications of the UK NQCC testbed and the New Mexico testbed?
How will the gigaquop system's 2028-2029 internal-use window interact with Libra's 2028 cloud deployment?
In sources reviewed, 2026 QuEra/Harvard output was mostly theory and simulation; when will higher-distance or high-rate-code QEC experiments appear?

IonQ.summary: IonQ's roadmap, restated across its June 2025 blog, roadmap page and later releases, targets about 10,000 physical qubits on one chip and about 800 logical qubits in 2027, 20,000 physical and 1,600 logical qubits in 2028, and about 2,000,000 physical qubits with 40,000 to 80,000 logical qubits and logical error below 1e-12 by 2030. Public results include #AQ 64 on Tempo (2025), a 99.99% two-qubit gate result on a two-ion prototype (October 2025), a post-selected qLDPC memory experiment at roughly breakeven on 40 ions (2026), and photonic entanglement of two commercial systems (April 2026). On 8 September 2026 IonQ launched Superion 256 (deliveries 2027) and announced Superion 10K (lab target 2027). The Walking Cat architecture, a CPU decoder benchmarked on 408 logical qubits, and resource estimates are published, but no logical-gate or magic-state hardware demonstration was found. IonQ entered DARPA QBI Stage B in November 2025; no IonQ statement on the DOE Q Competition was found.

items.name: Walking Cat architecture
items.claim: 'We propose a fault-tolerant quantum computer architecture for trapped-ion devices, which we call the walking cat architecture. Our blueprint includes a compiler, a detailed description of all the quantum error-correction protocols, a micro-architecture, a sufficiently fast decoder, and thorough simulations.' It is based entirely on LDPC codes and a cat factory that supplies cat states for logical operations.

changes.change: IonQ publishes its 'accelerated roadmap': 10,000 physical qubits on one chip in 2027, two interconnected chips (20,000 physical) in 2028, and over 2,000,000 physical qubits translating to 40,000 to 80,000 logical qubits by 2030 with logical error below 1e-12.

Analyst Day detail: a 256-qubit electronic-control processor in 2026; 10,000 physical qubits providing 800 logical qubits below 1e-7 error in 2027 (12:1); 2 million qubits in 2030 at a bill-of-materials cost under $30 million.
IonQ says the 99.99% prototypes 'will form the basis for its 256-qubit systems that will be demonstrated in 2026'.
The 2030 logical-qubit target is stated as a single figure of 80,000 in the Q3 2025 and QBI releases, where the June 2025 blog gave 40,000 to 80,000.

The Walking Cat architecture is published as the blueprint IonQ later says the 10K hardware is the first generation built to run; its dense configuration (2,514 physical qubits for 110 logical) implies a higher overhead than the roadmap's 12.5 to 1.
SkyWater acquisition closes (31 Jul 2026), bringing a foundry in house; first fully integrated 256-qubit QPUs are reported back from fabrication and under test.

Framing of the 256-qubit step moves from 'demonstrated in 2026' (Oct 2025) to 'available to order now, with customer deliveries in 2027' (Superion release) and 'begin commissioning 256-qubit systems in 2027' (Q2 call). No explicit slip of a dated target was announced.

The 10,000-qubit system is described as reaching 'full fault tolerance reality in a 2027 lab setting' and 'manufacturable, commercial reality in 2028'; the explicit 2028 commercial date is new relative to the roadmap rows read.

Interconnect timing differs between versions: the June 2025 blog places two interconnected chips and networking in 2028, while the roadmap page (undated, read 1 Oct 2026) lists photonic interconnect as introduced in 2029.

assessments.who: PostQuantum.com (Marin Ivezic), on the qLDPC breakeven preprint
assessments.point: Calls it the first qLDPC breakeven on any platform but notes 74.8% of BB5 [[30,4,5]] shots were discarded for leakage ('A 75% rejection rate is not compatible with operational error correction'), larger BB5 codes did worse than smaller ones, and the result does not match Google's surface-code distance scaling or the logical-qubit scale of Quantinuum's Helios, as the author characterizes them.

assessments.who: PostQuantum.com (Marin Ivezic), on the Walking Cat architecture
assessments.point: States there is 'no experimental demonstration of any component of the walking cat architecture', that QCCD operation has been shown on devices of up to 98 qubits versus about 2,500 needed (a 25-fold scale-up), and that 'near term' buildability is an aspiration, not an engineering fact.

assessments.who: PostQuantum.com (Marin Ivezic), on the 99.99% gate result
assessments.point: Reads the headline as a two-ion subspace randomized-benchmarking result, 'not yet at 256-qubit scale', with crosstalk, spectator modes, mode crowding, calibration drift and correlated errors in large arrays still to be shown.

assessments.who: Quantum Computing Report, on IonQ's 2025 Analyst Day roadmap
assessments.point: Notes that 'the company will need to continue to execute to stay on track with their roadmap because quantum is a very competitive industry'.

assessments.who: DARPA, QBI program status page (10 Mar 2026)
assessments.point: Reports eleven organizations in Stage B and two US2QC performers in Stage C, and does not name IonQ on that page; it is a status statement, not an assessment of IonQ's roadmap.

open_questions: Has the 256-qubit Superion chip been operated at full array size, and what are its array-wide two-qubit fidelity, qubit count in use and connectivity? No public data were found as of 30 Sep 2026.

Does the 99.99% two-qubit result, measured on a two-ion prototype with subspace randomized benchmarking, carry over to multi-ion zones with crosstalk, and how does it compare with the 99.3% to 99.5% fidelities reported on Forte-generation systems?

How is the roadmap's 12.5 physical-per-logical ratio (10,000 to 800) reconciled with the Walking Cat dense configuration of 2,514 physical qubits for 110 logical (about 23 per logical, computed) and with the 408-logical-qubit decoder benchmark?

What does '<1e-7 logical error' mean on the roadmap page (per logical operation, per cycle or per algorithm), given that public logical error is about 1e-2 per cycle with 19% to 75% of shots discarded?
When will hardware logical gates, cat-state factories and magic-state preparation be demonstrated, given that the breakeven experiment contains none of them?

Will IonQ's real-time decoder be run on live hardware syndromes? Its 408-logical-qubit benchmark (arXiv 2608.25027) is a circuit-level simulation in which the 31.5 million figure counts syndrome-extraction cycles; the workload includes 555,130 T gates, above DOE's illustrative 10^5 hard operations for a first-generation system.
Will IonQ apply to the DOE Quantum Genesis Q Competition (applications due 19 Oct 2026), and which system and 2028 deliverable would it propose? No IonQ statement was found.
Has IonQ been selected for DARPA QBI Stage C? None announced as of the 5 Aug 2026 call.
Will IonQ release raw QEC experiment data, or code for its real-time decoder and Walking Cat compiler? Its public code so far includes the beam-search decoder used in the breakeven experiment.

recs: A phased initiative: Quantum Grand Challenges, then a DOE Quantum Computing User Facility, then integration across DOE science.
Quantum Grand Challenges: milestone-driven competitions toward a scientifically relevant, error-corrected capability by 2028.
New partnership models for co-design: embedded fellowships, joint appointments, shared prototypes, lower IP barriers.
Embed quantum across all relevant Office of Science programs and couple it to HPC, AI and user facilities.
Broaden investment across the technology stack, including real-time error correction and decoding, and the computing-sensing interface.
Sustain national investment commensurate with the opportunity.

IBM.verdict: First-generation scale in 2029, a year after DOE's evaluation. Strongest on integration and pre-fault-tolerant science; no hardware logical qubit on its codes yet.

clock.label: Kookaburra: first qLDPC memory module (12 logical qubits per gross code)

LQ.t: 12 logical qubits per gross-code module in simulation. Loon, the first test chip, was due for assembly at the end of 2025, and no hardware logical memory on these codes has been published.

LO.t: Magic-state factories designed in simulation; the first multi-module injection is planned for 2028.

AR.t: In simulation, 12 logical qubits survive about a million cycles on 288 qubits; no hardware logical error rate yet.

SC.t: Relay-BP decodes in under 480 ns on an AMD FPGA, not yet inside a logical-qubit experiment.

SI.t: Quantum-centric supercomputing at RIKEN (with Fugaku) and Cleveland Clinic; open-source Slurm and QRMI plugins. Pre-fault-tolerant systems.

SV.t: Three of the report's state-of-the-art results ran on IBM Heron processors: a 12,635-atom protein-ligand complex, fusion-blanket molten salts, and KCuF₃ spectra checked against neutron data. All pre-fault-tolerant.

S3.t: Fusion-blanket FLiBe molten-salt clusters on up to 66 qubits, within 0.7 kcal/mol of full CI (with ORNL, 2026).

LQ.t: 48 error-detected logical qubits (2023); dozens of error-corrected logical qubits in deep circuits on up to 448 atoms (Harvard-led, 2025).

LO.t: Logical 5-to-1 distillation lifted magic-state fidelity from 95.1% to 99.4% at distance 3 with post-selection; 48 error-detected CCZ gates ran in one circuit.

AR.t: Distance-5 surface code at 0.62% per round, 2.14× below distance 3 in a four-round circuit; a 3,000-atom array ran for over two hours with reloading.

SC.t: All-to-all connectivity by moving atoms; 270 ns entangling gates but millisecond-scale cycles; qubit re-use raised cycle rate about 100×.

SI.t: On-premises system beside AIST's ABCI-Q supercomputer (2025); NERSC has had remote access since 2023.

SV.t: String breaking in a (2+1)D gauge theory (analog, 2025) and a Kitaev honeycomb spin liquid with built-in error detection (2025).

IonQ.verdict: The most aggressive dates: about 800 logical qubits in 2027 on paper. Public hardware shows memory only, a post-selected qLDPC breakeven on 40 ions.

clock.label: IonQ reports 99.99% two-qubit fidelity on a two-ion electronic-control prototype (21 Oct 2025).
IonQ reports qLDPC memories on 40 ions at about breakeven lifetime with post-selection (preprint first posted about June 2026).
IonQ launched Superion 256 on 8 Sep 2026 with QPUs fabricated and customer deliveries in 2027; no array-wide performance data are public.
The roadmap page lists 12 logical qubits at below 1e-7 logical error in 2026, near the DOE prototype's 10 logical qubits; no public data show it yet.
The roadmap lists 10,000 physical and about 800 logical qubits in 2027, with a 2027 lab setting for the 10K system and no stated hard-operation count.
The roadmap lists 20,000 physical qubits in two interconnected chips and 1,600 logical qubits in 2028, and IonQ also states commercial manufacturability for 2028.
The roadmap page lists 200,000 physical and 8,000 logical qubits in 2029, with photonic interconnect introduced.
IonQ targets over 2,000,000 physical and 40,000 to 80,000 logical qubits by 2030 with logical error below 1e-12.

LQ.t: A 40-ion experiment encodes 2 to 4 logical qubits per code block across eight codes at about breakeven lifetime with post-selection; no multi-block run with 10 or more logical qubits was reported in the summary read.

LO.t: The Walking Cat blueprint and a 408-logical-qubit decoder benchmark cover logical operations in design and simulation, but no logical gate or magic-state preparation on hardware was found.

AR.t: A 99.99% two-qubit gate result on a two-ion prototype and a post-selected breakeven memory are public, while production-generation systems report 99.3% to 99.5% two-qubit fidelity and array-wide fidelity for 256 qubits is unpublished.

SC.t: All-to-all gates on a 40-ion chain and photonic entanglement of two commercial systems are shown, but entanglement rate, fidelity and cycle speed at roadmap scale are not public.

SI.t: Forte Enterprise was commissioned at EPB on 18 Sep 2026, Superion 256 is sold to FIU and NVIDIA's NVAQC for 2027, and a CPU decoder is benchmarked, but no integrated fault-tolerant stack has been demonstrated.

SV.t: Pre-fault-tolerant hardware runs appear in a Nature Communications neutrinoless double-beta decay study and a 24-qubit catalysis workflow on Forte; no error-corrected science result is public.

open.t: Forte Enterprise runs on site at EPB in Chattanooga (launched 18 Sep 2026) and KISTI and QuantumBasel systems are described as deployed or in final assembly; Superion 256 installations at NVAQC and FIU are scheduled for 2027, and no IonQ system at a DOE laboratory was found.

OLCF's user documentation lists IonQ among four Quantum Computing User Program platforms, with Forte and Forte Enterprise 1 (#AQ 36 each) accessible through the IonQ Quantum Cloud under OLCF allocations; an IonQ researcher presented Forte results at an OLCF user call in December 2025.

IonQ systems are reachable through the IonQ Quantum Cloud, Amazon Braket, Azure Quantum and Google Cloud Marketplace, with Qiskit, Cirq and other SDKs. Users can submit circuits in IonQ's native gates (GPi, GPi2 and, on Forte systems, ZZ) with IonQ's compiler turned off; IonQ's documentation says the underlying Raman pulse implementation is not exposed.

The qiskit-ionq provider is Apache-2.0 but hosted by the community; IonQ's own GitHub organizations publish Apache-2.0 tools and a point-in-time archive that includes its beam-search qLDPC decoder. Neither organization hosts the real-time decoder or the Walking Cat compiler, and NVAQC workloads use the open CUDA-Q platform.

The breakeven, Walking Cat and real-time decoder papers are public preprints, and IonQ's GitHub publications archive hosts the beam-search decoder used in the breakeven experiment. The breakeven preprint has no data-availability statement, and the archive holds no raw syndrome or QEC experiment data.
IonQ entered Stage B in November 2025; DARPA's March 2026 page names no companies, and no Stage C selection for IonQ had been announced by the 5 Aug 2026 earnings call.

S1.t: An IonQ speaker presented a 24-qubit QC-AFQMC matchgate-shadow experiment on Forte for a transition-metal-catalyzed reaction workflow at an OLCF user call in December 2025, and IonQ cites an AstraZeneca workflow with a claimed 20x time-to-solution speedup; neither is error-corrected.

S2.t: No IonQ hardware run, error-detected run or fault-tolerant estimate for strongly correlated materials was found in the sources read.

S3.t: No IonQ demonstration or estimate for fusion materials or plasma was found in the sources read.

S4.t: A Nature Communications study ran neutrinoless double-beta decay of a simple nucleus in 1+1D QCD on Forte and Forte Enterprise with 32 qubits plus 4 flag qubits and 470 RZZ gates, reporting a 10-sigma lepton-number-violation signal.

S5.t: The same study is a toy-scale lattice-gauge-theory run on hardware with flag-qubit error detection, not a fault-tolerant field-theory calculation at the scale DOE's S5 describes.

gaps: No public hardware result shows logical gates or magic-state preparation on IonQ systems, so DOE's hard-operation counts of 10^3 for the prototype tier and 10^5 for the first-generation tier have no hardware baseline from IonQ.

IonQ's roadmap lists about 800 logical qubits in 2027 and 1,600 in 2028 but states no hard-operation target and no date by which a 100-logical-qubit machine would run a fault-tolerant algorithm, so it cannot be compared directly with DOE's September 2028 evaluation.
The best public logical error is about 1% to 3.5% per logical qubit per cycle after discarding 19% to 75% of shots for leakage, against a roadmap target of below 1e-7 for 2026 and 2027.

The 256-qubit and 10,000-qubit chips have no published array-wide gate fidelity, and the 99.99% figure comes from a two-ion prototype, so scaling of fidelity, calibration and ion transport is not yet shown in public data.

intro.title: Our roadmap to scientific fault tolerance
intro.lead: Ten milestones that turn four company roadmaps, community results and DOE's 2028 bar into work many groups can share. Each milestone has exit criteria an independent lab could check; progress is the share of those criteria met as of 1 October 2026.
method: The milestones are ordered by what DOE's tiers need first. The Prototype tier (10 logical qubits, 10³ hard operations, about a year after award) needs logic on real codes, a magic-state supply, a closed real-time loop and a shared way to measure them. The First-generation tier (100 logical qubits, 10⁵ hard operations, evaluated in September 2028) adds a compiled scientific workflow that finishes within 24 hours. The Next-generation tier (1,000 logical qubits, 10⁷ hard operations) and the facility scale the SCAC report describes (1,000 to 10,000 logical qubits, 10⁹ to 10¹⁰ hard operations) need modules that compute together, machines that calibrate themselves and software whose correctness is proven.

Each of the sixteen research problems in this analysis sits in exactly one milestone, and every reviewed paper, tool and program is classified through those problems. A milestone's progress counts its exit criteria: a criterion met on public evidence counts fully, a criterion met in part counts half.

The exit criteria are this analysis's proposals, not DOE requirements. Where DOE gives a number (hard operations, logical qubits, 24-hour runs, independent validation), the criteria use it; where it does not, they set a threshold an outside laboratory could measure.

milestones.q: Can noisy machines produce scientific results that survive classical checking?
milestones.why: DOE's science roadmap asks for benchmark problems validated against classical methods or experiment before error-corrected hardware arrives. This bridge keeps users, workloads and classical baselines moving while logical machines are built, and it trains the adversarial checking that later claims will face.
milestones.state: In July 2026 three IBM-linked advantage claims on 56 to 97 qubits were posted for open challenge, alongside Google's 65-qubit Quantum Echoes result from 2025, and a partial classical rebuttal appeared within weeks. HPC-coupled methods such as sample-based diagonalization reached 77 qubits with Fugaku, and a study with Oak Ridge and Los Alamos scored IBM Heron simulations of KCuF₃ against neutron-scattering spectra. Provable error bars at this scale do not yet exist.

exit.t: A beyond-classical claim survives at least two independent classical attacks at full scale.
exit.n: The July 2026 claims are mid-cycle; the first rebuttal (frozen-tree sampling) targets a statistical loophole rather than the structured task.

exit.t: HPC-coupled methods report error bars validated against exact, experimental or certified references at 50 or more qubits.
exit.n: KCuF₃ spectra on 50 qubits were scored against neutron data; convergence proofs for randomized sample-based diagonalization are at an early stage.

exit.t: A neutral, timed process adjudicates claims and rebuttals.
exit.n: IBM's open advantage tracker invites challenges, but no neutral body sets timelines or rules.

works.by: IBM with the University of Chicago
works.c: Certified a fidelity lower bound of 0.284 for doped-Clifford sampling on 97 qubits, from 2,051 accepted samples.
Measured out-of-time-order correlators on 65 qubits, reported as about 13,000 times faster than an estimated Frontier run.

works.by: Quantinuum, JPMorganChase, Argonne and Oak Ridge
works.c: Certified 71,313 bits of entropy from a 56-qubit H2 run, with classical verification on 1.1 ExaFLOPS of aggregate compute.
Sample-based diagonalization on up to 77 qubits with Fugaku for N₂ dissociation and iron-sulfur clusters.

works.by: IBM with Oak Ridge and Los Alamos
works.c: Scored Heron simulations of KCuF₃ and an XXZ chain against inelastic neutron-scattering spectra with several distance metrics.
Matched IBM's 2023 127-qubit utility experiment with converged classical simulation, a model for adversarial checking.
Posted a classical attack on statistical verification within weeks of the July 2026 claims.
Presents a convergence-proof framework for randomized sample-based diagonalization.

combos.d: Converged tensor-network rebuttals and supercomputer-verified randomness show how a classical referee can work. Run on DOE leadership computers under a fixed time window, they would turn today's claim-and-rebuttal cycle into an adjudicated process.

Convergence proofs for randomized diagonalization, the published failure modes of quantum-selected methods and neutron-scattering references together define when an HPC-coupled result can carry a trustworthy error bar.

collab.t: DOE computing facilities with hardware makers
collab.d: Run the classical side of every major advantage claim on Frontier-class machines within an agreed window, so claims are settled in months rather than argued indefinitely.

collab.t: Chemistry and materials theorists with HPC-coupled algorithm teams
collab.d: Turn sample-based diagonalization results into certified bounds on the molecules and materials DOE names.

gaps.t: No verification standard spans sampling, echo, randomness and peaked-circuit protocols, so each claim is argued on its own terms.
No sample-based method yet has a provable, non-exponential error bound at 50 or more qubits.

IBM.h: Three 2026 hardware claims posted openly for classical challenge

Google.h: Quantum Echoes claim (65 qubits) plus RCS verification theory

QuEra.h: 2023 logical-qubit IQP sampling remains the reference result

IonQ.h: No public IonQ work on certifying beyond-classical results found.

Community.h: Very active: independent groups match or rebut most claims within months

milestones.name: Shared yardstick
milestones.q: Can an independent laboratory measure a logical machine the same way on every platform?
milestones.why: DOE will agree an objective methodology with each Q Competition awardee and pays Prototype awards only once a milestone is validated, so the yardstick has to exist before the first Prototype claim is checked.
milestones.state: Each company reports logical performance in its own units: Google publishes logical error per cycle with open data, QuEra moved to operation budgets (megaquop and gigaquop), IBM counts gates on logical qubits, and IonQ reports breakeven after discarding 19% to 75% of shots for leakage. Community tools such as logical randomized benchmarking, application suites and the Metriq platform supply parts of a standard. DARPA's QBI, IEEE P7131 and DOE's $45M V&V testbed call are the institutional routes, and none has published a cross-vendor result.

exit.t: One open protocol reports hard operations completed reliably, logical error per operation and the discard rate, and runs unmodified on at least two modalities.
exit.n: Logical randomized benchmarking and volumetric frameworks exist, but no protocol counts hard operations across modalities.

exit.t: Every logical-qubit claim reports unconditional and post-selected error separately.
exit.n: Recent Google, Quantinuum and IonQ papers state discard rates; operation-budget metrics have no verification protocol.

exit.t: A third-party laboratory reproduces one vendor's logical claim end to end.
exit.n: DOE's V&V testbed awards are expected in winter 2026–27, and DARPA's QBI IV&V milestone is due in December 2026.

works.c: Distance-7 surface-code memory at 0.143% error per cycle (Λ = 2.14), with the data released; the clearest public logical-level report.
Distance-7 logical error of 7.72×10⁻⁴ per cycle and up to 3.5× better drift stability under reinforcement-learning control.
Ran 48 error-corrected and up to 94 error-detected logical qubits on the 98-qubit Helios.
Logical error 4.7× to 800× below physical depending on the code, a claim that drew scrutiny over post-selection.
qLDPC memories at about breakeven on 40 ions, with the share of shots discarded for leakage stated.
Defined logical randomized benchmarking, a logical-level decay protocol independent of physical noise assumptions.
Reviewed benchmarks from the physical to the application level, the methods base for DOE-style V&V.
Specified the five components any volumetric benchmark needs.

combos.d: Logical randomized benchmarking supplies the decay protocol, the volumetric framework supplies the rules for width, depth and success, and Google's released syndrome data give a public test set. Joined, they would count hard operations completed reliably on data anyone can check.

Helios, IonQ's breakeven run and the Microsoft–Atom Computing experiment each mix detection, correction and discarding differently. A shared table that separates detected, corrected and discarded shots would make their logical-qubit counts comparable.

collab.t: A laboratory-led V&V team with vendors of different modalities
collab.d: DOE's V&V call requires an Office of Science laboratory lead and at least two collaborators from outside the DOE and NNSA laboratories. A Berkeley Lab- or Oak Ridge-led team that adds Sandia's benchmarking group and a superconducting, an atom and an ion vendor would produce the first cross-modality protocol.

collab.t: DARPA QBI and IEEE P7131 on one set of definitions
collab.d: Aligning metric definitions lets one report serve both programs and DOE's evaluation.

gaps.t: No agreed treatment of post-selection, leakage or loss in reported logical error.
Operation budgets (megaquop, gigaquop, 10⁸ gates) have no verification protocol and no stated hard-operation share.

IBM.h: Announced a 2029 gate-count target with no public verification protocol yet.

Google.h: Most detailed public logical-level reporting among the three companies.

QuEra.h: Redefined reporting around operation budgets instead of logical-qubit counts.

IonQ.h: Physical-level #AQ benchmark plus one post-selected logical breakeven comparison; no verification protocol.

Community.h: Supplies the shared metrics and platforms vendor claims get checked against.

milestones.name: Predictable noise floor
milestones.q: Can we predict and hold the logical noise floor as machines grow?
milestones.why: Ten to the fifth reliable hard operations need logical error near 10⁻⁶ per operation, and the Q Competition asks each applicant for its logical noise floor. That floor is set by correlated, drifting and non-Pauli errors that appear only at scale.
milestones.state: Google learns from syndromes on live hardware, through decoder priors, AlphaQubit and a 2026 reinforcement-learning loop that held a distance-7 memory at 7.72×10⁻⁴ per cycle. Leakage removal on transmons cut leakage from about 1% to 0.1%, and Harvard and QuEra ran a 3,000-atom array continuously for over two hours with reloading. IonQ's 2026 qLDPC experiment still discarded 19% to 75% of shots on detected leakage, a gap-engineered transmon array still shows correlated phase-error bursts about once every 71 seconds, and no learned model forecasts logical error with calibrated uncertainty on a new code or scale.

exit.t: A syndrome-learned model predicts logical error on held-out circuits within a factor of two at 100 or more qubits, with stated uncertainty.
exit.n: Decoding graphs are learned from experiments and sparse Pauli-Lindblad models scale to 100+ qubits, but no calibrated forecast at a new scale has been published.

exit.t: Leakage and loss are detected and decoded with no more than 10% of shots discarded.
exit.n: Atom reloading and transmon leakage removal work on hardware; the trapped-ion qLDPC run discarded up to 75%.

exit.t: A decoder or scheduler response suppresses burst-driven logical error spikes on hardware.
exit.n: Bursts are characterized (rare correlated events about once an hour on Willow, phase-error bursts about every 71 s in a gap-engineered array), but no hardware response has been shown.

works.c: Online reinforcement-learning control from syndromes during a distance-7 experiment.
Optimized decoder priors from data, lowering logical error against uniform priors on hardware.
Recovered decoding-graph structure and weights directly from experimental syndrome statistics.
Polynomial-scaling noise characterization of syndrome-extraction circuits.
Decoding with measured syndrome correlations instead of assumed noise.
Cut average leakage population from about 1% to 0.1% during error correction.
Ran a 3,000-atom array coherently and continuously for over two hours with reloading.
Atom-loss-aware decoding with about three orders of magnitude lower logical error than a naive decoder.
In a gap-engineered array, correlated phase-error bursts still occur about once every 71 s, with frequency shifts up to 3 MHz lasting about 1 ms.
Leakage speculation with up to 3× fewer false alarms across surface, color and qLDPC codes.

combos.d: Public syndrome data, decoding-graph estimation, scalable circuit characterization and noise-aware decoding are the four parts of a model that forecasts logical error. Trained on one platform's released data and tested on another's, it would give the logical noise floor DOE asks applicants to state.

combos.t: One decoder for leakage, loss and erasure
combos.d: Loss-aware decoding for atoms, leakage speculation for transmons and qLDPC codes, dual-rail erasure qubits and chain-loss correction for ions solve the same problem four ways. A common decoder interface would let each platform reuse the others' advances.

collab.t: Hardware makers releasing raw syndrome data to noise-learning groups
collab.d: Google already publishes; IBM, QuEra and IonQ do not. Released data would let outside groups model IBM's long-range couplers, atom loss and ion leakage.

collab.t: Materials and radiation physicists with superconducting teams
collab.d: Fermilab's SQMS center works on coherence and materials; joining it with Google's and IBM's burst data targets detection and decoder response to correlated bursts.

gaps.t: No calibrated logical-error forecast for unseen codes or scales.
No published leakage or loss treatment for IBM's long-range c-coupler circuits.
Trapped-ion qLDPC runs discard up to three quarters of shots, which operational error correction cannot afford.

IBM.h: Sparse Pauli-Lindblad learning at 100+ qubits, for mitigation rather than syndromes

Google.h: On-hardware decoder calibration, ML decoding, and RL-based drift control from syndromes

QuEra.h: Leads neutral-atom loss detection, continuous reloading, and loss-aware decoding at thousand-qubit scale

IonQ.h: Leakage detection with post-selection run on hardware; chain loss and leakage handling simulated.

Community.h: Broad industry-and-academic ecosystem builds dual-rail/erasure hardware and loss/leakage-aware decoding theory

milestones.name: Logic on real codes
milestones.q: Can logical gates run on the high-rate codes each platform has chosen?
milestones.why: Every DOE tier counts logical operations, not memories. IBM, QuEra and IonQ have all bet on high-rate codes to fit 100 or more logical qubits into their 2027–2029 machines, and the Prototype tier already asks for 10 logical qubits running 10³ hard operations.
milestones.state: Theory moved fast: surgery with near-linear overhead (gauging, SSIP, extractors), complete instruction sets for bicycle and SHYPS codes, and 2025–26 proposals for parallel operations at about twice the memory cost. Hardware lags: logic has run on small codes (48 error-detected logical qubits with CCZ gates on atoms, a four-logical-qubit GHZ state on ions, color-code teleportation on Willow), and the first high-rate memories on hardware, a [[18,4,4]] code at 8.9% error per cycle and IonQ's codes at breakeven with post-selection, have no logical gates between blocks.

exit.t: A logical measurement or gate between two high-rate code blocks on hardware, decoded in real time, with error below the physical baseline.
exit.n: No hardware logical operation between qLDPC blocks has been published.

exit.t: Ten or more logical qubits in one circuit on a code with higher rate than the surface code, completing 10³ logical operations.
exit.n: Harvard and QuEra ran 48 error-detected logical qubits in [[8,3,2]] blocks with 228 two-qubit and 48 CCZ gates; Helios ran 48 error-corrected logical qubits. Neither reached 10³ hard operations.

exit.t: For each major platform, a code-circuit pair that beats the surface code at equal circuit-level error under that platform's constraints.
exit.n: Simulated pairs exist for superconducting grids, atoms and ions; hardware validation is limited to small memories.

works.c: Gross code: 12 logical qubits in 288 physical qubits for about a million cycles in simulation, against about 3,000 for a surface code.

works.by: IBM with Oxford, Sydney and MIT
works.c: Extractors: one logical cycle of O(d) syndrome rounds per Pauli measurement on any qLDPC code.

works.by: Caltech and the University of Chicago
works.c: High-rate surgery: hundreds of simultaneous logical measurements at about twice the memory's space-time cost.
SHYPS codes: a [[225,16,8]] code performs like a distance-7 surface-code layout with 3.5× fewer qubits, and depth-126 logical circuits stay near memory performance (simulation).
48 logical qubits with 228 logical two-qubit gates and 48 CCZ gates on up to 280 atoms.
Color code on Willow: transversal Cliffords add 0.27% error; lattice-surgery teleportation at 86.5–90.7% fidelity.
Four logical qubits entangled beyond break-even in a non-local code (GHZ fidelity 99.5–99.7%).
A [[18,4,4]] high-rate code on superconducting hardware at 8.91% error per logical qubit per cycle.
qLDPC memories with two to four logical qubits per block at about breakeven on 40 ions, with post-selection.
Walking Cat: cat-state logical measurements and a six-instruction logical set for trapped-ion qLDPC memories, in simulation.
A [[540,108,18]] code reaches about 10¹⁰ simulated logical operations with two failures.
Tile codes for planar chips; [[512,18,19]] reported more than 12× better than the rotated surface code.

combos.d: Extractors give a logical instruction set; 2D-local, morphing and Louvre circuits cut the connectivity bicycle codes need. Together they define a logical measurement IBM-style hardware could run on a gross-code block.

Batched high-rate operations, homological product codes and movement-aware qLDPC layouts all assume reconfigurable atom arrays. Combined, they specify transversal and batched logic on a high-rate code that an atom array can execute.
The Walking Cat instruction set, codes designed for long ion chains and automated surgery would together target a logical Pauli measurement between two blocks on one ion chain.

collab.t: Code theorists embedded with hardware teams
collab.d: Most gadget theory comes from universities (Oxford, Sydney, MIT, Caltech, Chicago, Yale), while the hardware sits with IBM, QuEra, IonQ and Quantinuum. Embedded fellowships and joint appointments, which the SCAC report recommends, shorten the path from gadget to experiment.

collab.t: Decoder teams in the same loop
collab.d: Surgery changes the detector graph over time, so each gadget needs a decoder developed with it.

gaps.t: No hardware logical operation between qLDPC blocks.
Most gadget proofs are phenomenological; circuit-level fault distance is rarely certified.
who: verification groups at Maryland and Chicago

gaps.t: Codes optimized for memory may lack cheap logic, and searches rarely score logical operations.

IBM.h: Leads qLDPC gadget theory; Kookaburra LPU module targeted for 2026, no hardware logic yet

Google.h: Time-dynamic surface-code circuits relax hardware needs on hardware; no qLDPC search

QuEra.h: Theory for transversal and batched high-rate logic; hardware logic so far on small codes

IonQ.h: Ion-chain-tailored BB5 codes designed; nine codes run on a 40-ion barium chain.

Community.h: Photonic, Xanadu, Oxford, Caltech/Oratomic and others drive gadgets; small hardware demos

milestones.name: Magic at rate
milestones.q: Can machines supply enough high-fidelity magic states for 10⁵ hard operations in a day?
milestones.why: DOE counts hard operations: 10³ for a Prototype and 10⁵ for the First generation, within a 24-hour end-to-end run. That is more than one accepted magic state per second, sustained, at an error low enough that the whole run succeeds.
milestones.state: Logical magic states have beaten their physical counterparts on hardware three times: Google's cultivation reached state fidelity 0.9999 while keeping 8% of attempts, Quantinuum's logical controlled-Hadamard gate reached infidelity at most 2.3×10⁻⁴ against 10⁻³ physical, and Harvard and QuEra distilled logical magic states from 95.1% to 99.4% fidelity with post-selection, above the 98.9% of the physical magic state. Theory offers cultivation at roughly the cost of a CNOT, constant-overhead distillation and the first qLDPC-native factories, but each result is one protocol on one platform, and no machine has produced magic states continuously.

exit.t: A magic state on hardware with logical error below the physical two-qubit error.
exit.n: Google (cultivation) and Quantinuum (logical controlled-Hadamard) crossed this line in 2025; Harvard and QuEra's distilled states (99.4%, post-selected) beat the 98.9% physical magic state.

exit.t: One benchmark compares cultivation, distillation and injection in qubit-rounds per accepted state, under a shared noise model, on at least two platforms.
exit.n: Protocols are compared only within their own papers.

exit.t: Sustained production of more than one accepted magic state per second at 10⁻⁶ error or better, enough for 10⁵ hard operations in 24 hours.
exit.n: No machine has produced magic states continuously.

works.c: Cultivation: T states at 2×10⁻⁹ error at 10⁻³ physical noise for roughly the qubit-rounds of a lattice-surgery CNOT.
Cultivation on hardware: error reduced 40-fold to state fidelity 0.9999, keeping 8% of attempts.
Logical controlled-Hadamard infidelity at most 2.3×10⁻⁴ against 10⁻³ physical; magic-state infidelity 7×10⁻⁵ at 14.8% discard.
Logical 5-to-1 distillation lifted magic-state fidelity from 95.1% to 99.4% with distance-3 color codes and post-selection.
Magic tricycles: qLDPC-native magic states at 6×10⁻¹⁰ or better with modest post-selection on 50–100-qubit codes.
Distillation in the bicycle architecture at space-time volume comparable to the best surface-code factories.
In-situ injection on arbitrary CSS qLDPC codes: 1.62×10⁻³ per logical qubit at 10⁻³ noise on [[144,12,12]].

works.by: University of Sydney and Hebrew University
works.c: Cultivation with more than 20× higher generation rate under realistic noise.
Constant-overhead magic-state distillation (overhead exponent γ = 0) through algebraic-geometry codes.
qLDPC codes with transversal non-Clifford gates and near-linear dimension.

combos.d: Cultivation is cheap on surface-code patches; in-situ injection and bicycle-architecture distillation show how high-rate memories can receive the result. Joined, they define a factory that IBM-, IonQ- and QuEra-style machines can host.

combos.t: One cost benchmark for magic states
combos.d: Cultivation, zero-level distillation, redundant-ancilla preparation and tricycles each report cost differently. Re-implemented in the same simulator under one noise model, they would give qubit-rounds per accepted state on a single scale.

collab.t: Factory theorists with three hardware platforms
collab.d: Running the same protocol on superconducting, ion and atom hardware separates protocol cost from platform noise.

collab.t: Compiler groups for factory scheduling
collab.d: Factories compete with routing for space and time, so production has to be scheduled with the program.

gaps.t: No machine has produced magic states continuously.
No cross-platform cost benchmark for magic-state protocols.
Good-distance qLDPC codes with transversal non-Clifford gates remain an open coding problem.

IBM.h: Strong qLDPC code theory; no public hardware factory yet

Google.h: Cultivation theory (2024) and first hardware demonstration (2025)

QuEra.h: Theoretical qLDPC factories, plus a first hardware distillation demo

IonQ.h: Two H-type magic-state factory designs for qLDPC codes; simulation only.

Community.h: Very active: cost-model refinements, qLDPC constructions, cheaper protocols

milestones.name: Real-time loop
milestones.q: Can decoding and feed-forward keep pace with logical operations?
milestones.why: Every hard operation done by injection needs feed-forward, so even the Prototype tier's 10³ hard operations need a closed real-time loop, and correlated decoding of high-rate codes has to keep up at First-generation scale.
milestones.state: Real-time decoding of surface-code memories works on hardware: Willow decoded a distance-5 memory with 63 µs average latency at 1.1 µs cycles, and Riverlane's decoder answered within 9.6 µs on Rigetti qubits and closed a 6.9 µs loop with Qblox on emulated measurement data. For high-rate codes, IBM's Relay-BP decodes the gross code on AMD FPGAs, IonQ simulates real-time decoding of 408 logical qubits on one CPU, and NVIDIA's NVQLink reports 3.96 µs GPU round trips. Feed-forward of a magic-state injection inside one logical cycle has not been shown, and correlated decoding for transversal gates and qLDPC surgery still runs offline.

exit.t: Live decoding of the platform's own code during logical operations, with throughput above the syndrome rate and no backlog over 10⁶ rounds.
exit.n: Met for surface-code memories on Willow; qLDPC decoding meets FPGA deadlines but not inside a logical experiment.

exit.t: Feed-forward of a magic-state injection within one logical cycle on hardware.
exit.n: No hardware demonstration found.

exit.t: One controller-decoder interface used by at least two hardware vendors.
exit.n: NVQLink launched with 17 hardware builders and Riverlane's decoder runs with several, but neither is an agreed standard.

works.c: Real-time decoding at distance 5: 63 µs average latency at 1.1 µs cycles, with no backlog.
Relay-BP: belief propagation that matches matching on surface codes and beats BP+OSD on bicycle codes.
Real-time gross-code decoding on AMD FPGAs.
Mean decode under 1 µs per round and 9.6 µs response over nine rounds on superconducting qubits.
A full loop at 6.886 µs for Surface-17 and 11.886 µs for Surface-161, run on emulated measurement data.

works.by: NVIDIA with Berkeley Lab, Sandia and Oak Ridge
works.c: NVQLink: 3.96 µs maximum GPU–QPU round trip.
RISC-Q (DAC 2026): an open generator of RISC-V-programmable control systems-on-chip; its RFSoC prototype runs at 500 MHz with 16 DACs and 8 ADCs.
An open-source QEC system built on RISC-Q: 446 ns end-to-end decoding-feedback latency at distance 3 in loopback tests (IEEE QCE 2026).
Real-time decoding simulated for 408 logical qubits on a single CPU.
Correlated decoding of transversal circuits lowers logical error against per-patch decoding.
Ambiguity Clustering: qLDPC decoding 27–150× faster than BP-OSD.

works.by: University of Chicago and University of Michigan
works.c: SWIPER speculative window decoding (ISCA 2025) cuts simulated program runtimes by 40% on average against earlier parallel window decoders.

combos.d: Relay-BP, Ambiguity Clustering, localized statistics decoding and GPU decoding target the same codes on different hardware. One workload measured on FPGA, CPU and GPU for latency, throughput and accuracy would tell each roadmap what its decoder can sustain.
Open FPGA control stacks (QubiC, RISC-Q), a sub-microsecond open QEC system, NVQLink and improved injection protocols are the parts of a T gate by injection with correction inside one cycle.
Correlated decoding for transversal gates and its faster variant, combined with parallel and speculative windows, would bring transversal atom-array circuits into real time.

collab.t: Neutral decoder suppliers with every platform
collab.d: Riverlane and NVIDIA already work across hardware makers; IBM pairs with AMD in house. A shared benchmark lets each platform choose on evidence.

collab.t: National laboratories as integration testbeds
collab.d: Berkeley Lab, Sandia and Oak Ridge co-wrote NVQLink, and DOE's V&V testbed evaluates control-stack integration and execution times.

gaps.t: No cross-vendor real-time decoding benchmark.
No feed-forward for non-Clifford operations within one cycle on hardware.
Correlated decoding for transversal gates and qLDPC surgery runs offline.

IBM.h: Relay-BP plus FPGA demo bring real-time decoding to qLDPC gross-code memories (2025)

Google.h: Willow proved real-time hardware decoding; Tesseract and AlphaQubit 2 push accuracy/speed in simulation

QuEra.h: Correlated-decoding theory for transversal neutral-atom algorithms; roadmap ties fast decoding to NVIDIA

IonQ.h: Beam-search qLDPC decoders benchmarked in software on simulated data; no live hardware decoding.

Community.h: Dense open ecosystem of FPGA/GPU matching, BP and neural decoders outside the three roadmap vendors

milestones.name: Self-running machines
milestones.q: Can machines with ten thousand or more qubits calibrate and recover themselves during a run?
milestones.why: DOE judges progress by whether a system can operate reliably, repeatedly and at sufficient throughput, and a 24-hour First-generation run cannot stop for manual retuning. Machines of 10,000 or more qubits cannot be kept in tune by hand.
milestones.state: Closed-loop calibration now runs during error correction: Google's reinforcement-learning agent tuned over 1,000 parameters live in a distance-7 experiment, QuEra used an AI agent to recover laser locks in 695 of 700 trials, and a language-model agent brought up a 112-qubit processor autonomously. All of this is at hundreds of qubits; no calibration demonstration above about 1,000 qubits has been published, and vendors report calibration overhead in incompatible units.

exit.t: Closed-loop calibration holds logical error steady over a multi-hour run.
exit.n: Google reports up to 3.5× better drift stability; multi-hour logical data are not yet public.

exit.t: Autonomous bring-up and tune-up beyond 1,000 qubits, with published overhead scaling.
exit.n: The largest autonomous bring-up found is 112 qubits.

exit.t: At least 90% uptime with automated recovery across a 24-hour logical run.
exit.n: No such run has been reported.

works.c: A reinforcement-learning agent tuned over 1,000 parameters live during a distance-7 experiment.
An AI agent recovered laser locks in 695 of 700 trials, most in under 6 seconds.
Autonomous bring-up of a 112-qubit superconducting processor by a language-model agent.
Automated gate optimization across a full processor toward logical-qubit scale.
All-electronic trapped-ion control with sparse automated calibration in a seven-zone trap.
An open-source calibration framework, reported to cut calibration from hours to minutes.
Qibocal: open calibration for self-hosted devices, deployed on several independent processors.
Open AI models for calibration and error correction, launched in April 2026 with hardware partners.
First provable efficiency bounds for a self-calibrating fault-tolerance scheme.

combos.t: Calibration agents that optimize logical error
combos.d: Reinforcement learning from syndromes, open calibration stacks and open AI models for calibration point to one agent that tunes for logical error directly and runs on any vendor's control system.
Provable self-calibration, automated defect detection and fast frequency allocation are the ingredients of a calibration-overhead model that could be validated at 10⁴ qubits.

collab.t: Vendors with machine-learning teams
collab.d: Every closed-loop result so far pairs hardware with learning methods; outside AI groups need access to live control systems.

collab.t: Open testbeds for calibration research
collab.d: Berkeley Lab's AQT and Oak Ridge's on-site systems give researchers control access that commercial clouds do not; Sandia's open QSCOUT testbed is scheduled to close after fiscal 2026.

gaps.t: No calibration demonstration above about 1,000 qubits.
No agreed metric for calibration overhead and uptime.

IBM.h: TLS and coupler research underway; no published closed-loop demo at scale.

Google.h: First hardware demo of an RL agent tuning parameters live during QEC.

QuEra.h: AI agent automated one subsystem's recovery; full-array calibration not yet shown.

IonQ.h: Small-scale Oxford Ionics hardware shows sparse automated calibration; no AI or RL agents.

Community.h: Open frameworks plus agentic and ML calibration research are maturing quickly.

milestones.name: First scientific workflow
milestones.q: Can one DOE science problem be compiled, costed and run end to end at 100 logical qubits and 10⁵ hard operations?
milestones.why: This is DOE's First-generation bar for September 2028: a full scientific workflow on about 100 logical qubits with 10⁵ hard operations, finished within 24 hours and independently validated. The RFA asks every applicant to convert its roadmap to these units and to give hard and easy operation counts and wall-clock time for a demonstrator.
milestones.state: Resource estimators are plentiful (Qualtran, the Azure Quantum Resource Estimator, BenchQ, Rigetti's RRE and company tools from IBM, QuEra with Los Alamos, IonQ and Alice & Bob), but no study has reconciled three tools on one target, and estimates for the same molecule differ by orders of magnitude across architectures. Most published instances sit far above First-generation scale: FeMoco needs about four million physical qubits in Google's estimate, and IonQ's elliptic-curve blueprint needs 1,457 logical qubits and 39 million Toffoli gates. Compilers are near-optimal within single modalities, and CUDA-Q Logical is the first front end retargeted to more than one logical-code backend.

exit.t: For each of DOE's five science targets, one instance compiled to at most 100 logical qubits and 10⁵ hard operations, with its classical baseline stated.
exit.n: Published estimates for DOE-relevant targets sit well above 10⁵ hard operations; toy-scale hardware runs are not error-corrected.

exit.t: One compiler front end targets more than one logical-code backend under a shared cost model.
exit.n: CUDA-Q Logical (2026) retargets one front end; no shared cost model across lattice surgery, qLDPC and atom-array scheduling is agreed.

exit.t: Three independent estimators agree within a factor of two on one shared instance, with assumptions logged in a common format.
exit.n: No cross-tool reconciliation has been published; DARPA QBI's IV&V milestone is due in December 2026.

exit.t: A compiled workflow runs end to end within 24 hours on a logical machine and is validated against classical methods or experiment.
exit.n: Not yet possible on any machine.

works.c: Qualtran: an open library that costs algorithms down to qubits and wall-clock time.
Azure Quantum Resource Estimator: automatic logical and physical resource evaluation.
CUDA-Q Logical: one compiler front end retargeted to more than one logical-code backend.
Transversal STAR: a neutral-atom architecture for megaquop-scale simulation, about 10,000 physical qubits at 10⁻³ error in its surface-code version.
A fault-tolerant algorithm for electronic stopping power in fusion targets; classical data cut quantum resources by orders of magnitude.
Tensor hypercontraction: FeMoco with about four million physical qubits in under four days.
A fully compiled elliptic-curve estimate: 1,457 logical qubits and 39 million logical Toffoli gates.
A survey that consolidates per-algorithm resource claims into one comparable reference.
Near-optimal atom-array scheduling: 3.7× fewer gate stages than the prior baseline, scaling to 10,000 qubits.
SAT-based lattice-surgery synthesis that found an 8% smaller 15-to-1 T factory.
A five-stage framework for applications; naming concrete beyond-classical instances is the least funded stage.

combos.d: Qualtran, the Azure estimator, BenchQ and RRE encode different assumptions. Run on one DOE target through a shared assumption registry, they would give a reconciled estimate with stated uncertainty.

combos.t: The same workflow compiled for three architectures
combos.d: A retargetable front end, near-optimal atom-array scheduling, a resource-allocating lattice-surgery compiler and extractor scheduling for qLDPC codes cover the three main architectures. One workflow compiled through all of them under one cost model would make technology-neutral comparison concrete.
Google's application staging and published classical stress tests give a procedure for choosing First-generation instances whose classical baselines have already been defended.

collab.t: DOE domain scientists with resource-estimation teams
collab.d: Each of the five science targets (chemistry, materials, fusion, nuclear, particle physics) needs a domain owner who defends the instance and the classical baseline.

collab.t: Compiler groups across modalities
collab.d: Shared benchmarks and a cost model need compiler teams from each architecture working on the same programs.

gaps.t: No DOE science instance compiled to First-generation scale with a defended baseline.
No shared exchange format or cross-tool audit for resource estimates.
No open compiler benchmark at roadmap scale (200 or more logical qubits, about 10⁸ gates).
