QuEra.h: Bloqade compiles to atom-shuttling programs; roadmap sets high-rate-QEC targets.

IonQ.h: Single-platform logical instruction set and compiler designed; no cross-platform cost model.

Community.h: Broadest activity: algorithm design, dequantization, and cross-lab benchmarking

milestones.name: Modules that compute together
milestones.q: Can logical operations span modules joined by slower, noisier links?
milestones.why: IBM's Starling is built from linked modules, IonQ links chips from 2028, and Google's million-qubit milestone needs links. DOE's Next-generation tier of 1,000 logical qubits and the facility scale of 1,000 to 10,000 logical qubits are unlikely to fit in one module on most platforms.
milestones.state: Two-module links work on hardware: Oxford teleported a CZ gate between ion-trap modules at 86.2% fidelity, Harvard and AWS entangled memory nodes over 35 km of deployed fiber, IBM linked two processors with real-time classical communication, Duke and IonQ entangled three trapped-ion nodes, and an Argonne and Chicago two-chip router reached 96% average CZ fidelity. Threshold theory tolerates link errors near 10% against 1% in the bulk, but no fault-tolerant logical operation has spanned three or more real modules.

exit.t: A deterministic operation between two real modules with reported fidelity.
exit.n: Oxford's teleported CZ (86.2%), the Argonne–Chicago router (96% average CZ) and IBM's classically linked processors.

exit.t: A fault-tolerant logical operation spanning three or more real modules.
exit.n: Simulated only.

exit.t: Inter-module logical error within twice the intra-module logical error.
exit.n: No logical operation across modules has been measured.

exit.t: A shared cost model relating link rate and fidelity to logical error across modalities.
exit.n: Thresholds exist per architecture; no cross-modality model.

works.c: Teleported a CZ gate between ion-trap modules at 86.2% fidelity, with Bell pairs at 9.7 per second and 96.9% fidelity.
Entangled nanophotonic memory nodes over a 35 km deployed fiber loop.
Linked two processors with real-time classical communication into a 134-qubit graph state.
A two-chip superconducting processor with a reconfigurable router at 96% average CZ fidelity.
Tripartite entanglement of remote trapped-ion qubits across three nodes.
Error-corrected modules tolerate about 10% error at the interface against 1% in the bulk.
Distributed surface codes need an entanglement-to-decoherence rate ratio near 400, about 3× stricter than earlier estimates.
Optical interconnects for atom arrays: fault tolerance with local gate error below 1% and Bell-pair error below 10%.
Constant-rate entanglement distillation for an order-of-magnitude faster interconnect.
Aurora: 35 photonic chips networked into 86.4 billion entangled modes.

combos.t: A logical CNOT across modules with a link budget
combos.d: Transversal distributed operations, constant-rate distillation and the noisy-link thresholds together specify a logical CNOT between modules and the link rate and fidelity it needs.

combos.t: One chart for every link technology
combos.d: Ion photonic links, nanophotonic memory nodes, superconducting routers and microwave links report rate and fidelity in different ways. Placing them on one rate-versus-logical-error chart would show which architectures can meet the thresholds.

collab.t: Q-NEXT at Argonne as a neutral interconnect hub
collab.d: Q-NEXT's renewal centers on interconnects, with IBM, IonQ, Intel and university partners already in the center.

collab.t: Networking groups with error-correction theorists
collab.d: Link protocols and decoders across modules must be designed together.

gaps.t: No fault-tolerant operation across three or more real modules.
No shared cost model linking link rate and fidelity to logical error.

IBM.h: Two QPUs linked classically (2024); quantum L-couplers due 2027

Google.h: Targets ~1M-qubit interconnect via Milestone 6; little public link data

QuEra.h: Theory paper derives optical-link FT thresholds; no hardware inter-module demo yet

IonQ.h: Duke-IonQ three-node photonic entanglement and a two-system link; no logical operations across modules.

Community.h: Most active: threshold theory, distillation, and real two-module demos

milestones.name: Verified at production
milestones.q: Can we trust results that no classical computer can check?
milestones.why: First-generation runs can still be checked against classical results. Next-generation runs at 10⁷ hard operations and facility runs at 10⁹ to 10¹⁰ cannot, so trust has to come from machine-checked codes, decoders, compilers and algorithms.
milestones.state: Formal-methods groups have verified one layer at a time: a circuit optimizer (VOQC), production Qiskit compiler passes (Giallar), an end-to-end certified Shor implementation, lattice-surgery connectivity typing, fault-tolerance checks for codes up to 100 physical qubits and Clifford+T programs with few T gates. None of the four companies has published formal verification of its own fault-tolerant stack.

exit.t: Verified compiler passes and a fully verified end-to-end algorithm on unencoded circuits.
exit.n: VOQC, Giallar and the certified Shor implementation.

exit.t: A machine-checked distance certificate for a roadmap-scale qLDPC code.
exit.n: Distance verification is hard in general and has not been done at roadmap scale.

exit.t: A verified decoder: a proof of soundness for a decoder used in real time.
exit.n: No verified decoder found.

exit.t: A proof chain covering code, syndrome circuit, decoder, compiler and algorithm for one program on 100 or more logical qubits.
exit.n: Verification stops at small circuits and codes.

works.c: VOQC: the first fully machine-verified optimizer for real circuit-rewrite passes.
Giallar: push-button verification of production Qiskit compiler passes, which surfaced real bugs.
A formally certified end-to-end implementation of Shor's algorithm.
CoqQ: foundational verification of quantum programs that later work builds on.
Type-based static verification of lattice-surgery connectivity.
Fault-tolerance verification for systems up to 100 physical qubits, localizing error-propagation failures.
Efficient formal verification of error-correcting programs across 14 stabilizer codes.
Verified Toffoli decompositions, graph-state generators and the Steane encoder with lightweight proofs.
Symbolic execution that analyzes error-correcting codes beyond 1,000 qubits.

combos.d: Program-level QEC verification, fault-tolerance checking, symbolic execution and distance-verification bounds are the parts of a machine-checked distance and decoder-soundness result for a bicycle code.

combos.t: A proof chain through a fault-tolerant compiler
combos.d: A verified optimizer, lattice-surgery typing and a certified algorithm cover three layers; composing them would give one algorithm verified through a fault-tolerant compiler.

collab.t: Formal-methods groups with vendors' compiler and decoder teams
collab.d: No company has published verification of its own stack; academic groups need access to real compilers, decoders and code definitions.

collab.t: DOE V&V laboratories with formal-methods groups
collab.d: DOE's V&V call covers stack-wide verification across modalities, which can include machine-checked software.

gaps.t: No verified decoder.
Proof effort grows faster than system size, so verification stops at small circuits and codes.

IBM.h: No IBM-led verification work found; Qiskit itself is a third-party verification target.

Google.h: No Google-authored formal-verification publication targeting its FT stack was found.

QuEra.h: No QuEra-authored formal-verification publication targeting its FT stack was found.

IonQ.h: No public IonQ work on machine-checked guarantees for codes, decoders or compilers.

Community.h: Academic PL/formal-methods groups drive nearly all progress, one layer at a time.

gapClasses.name: Hard operations at rate
gapClasses.line: No machine has completed 10³ hard logical operations reliably; hardware magic states still come one at a time.
gapClasses.summary: DOE's tiers count hard operations, the non-Clifford steps that error-correcting codes make expensive: 10³ for a Prototype and 10⁵ for the First generation within a 24-hour run. On hardware, magic-state preparation has beaten the physical error only in single demonstrations, and none of the four company roadmaps states a hard-operation target.

evidence.t: Google's cultivation reached state fidelity 0.9999 on hardware while keeping 8% of attempts.
Quantinuum's logical controlled-Hadamard gate reached infidelity at most 2.3×10⁻⁴ against 10⁻³ for the physical gate.
Harvard and QuEra distilled logical magic states from 95.1% to 99.4% fidelity, with post-selection.
IBM's Starling plans 10⁸ gates with no stated non-Clifford share; QuEra's megaquop and IonQ's roadmap give no hard-operation count either.

gapClasses.why: A factory must reach very low error at an acceptance rate the machine can afford, on the code each platform uses. qLDPC-native factories exist only in simulation, and production has to be scheduled with routing and decoding in real time.
gapClasses.close: Sustained magic-state production above one accepted state per second at 10⁻⁶ error or better, measured with one cost benchmark on at least two platforms.
gapClasses.partners: Factory theorists (Google, Yale, Sydney, Harvard, Berkeley) working with hardware makers on three modalities, compiler groups for factory scheduling (UCLA, Chicago), and DOE V&V laboratories counting hard operations the same way for everyone.

gapClasses.name: Logic on high-rate codes
gapClasses.line: Three roadmaps depend on high-rate codes, but no logical gate between qLDPC blocks has run on hardware.
gapClasses.summary: High-rate codes are how IBM, QuEra and IonQ plan to fit 100 or more logical qubits into their 2027–2029 machines. Theory now offers complete instruction sets at about twice the memory's space-time cost, but on hardware high-rate memories exist only at small scale and none has performed a logical operation between blocks.

evidence.t: IBM's gross code holds 12 logical qubits in 288 physical qubits in simulation; no hardware logical memory on it has been published.
A [[18,4,4]] high-rate code ran on superconducting hardware at 8.91% error per logical qubit per cycle.
IonQ's qLDPC memories reached about breakeven on 40 ions after discarding 19% to 75% of shots.
High-rate surgery performs hundreds of simultaneous logical measurements at about twice the memory cost, in simulation.

gapClasses.why: Logic on qLDPC blocks needs long-range connectivity, below-threshold errors in both memory and ancilla systems, and decoders for detector graphs that change over time, all at once.
gapClasses.close: A logical measurement between two high-rate blocks on hardware, decoded in real time, with error below the physical baseline.
gapClasses.partners: University code theorists (Oxford, Sydney, MIT, Caltech, Chicago, Delft, Tsinghua) embedded with IBM, IonQ, QuEra and Quantinuum, with decoder teams (Riverlane, IBM's Relay-BP group) in the same loop.

gapClasses.name: Decoding that keeps up with logic
gapClasses.line: Decoders keep up with surface-code memories, not yet with logic on high-rate codes or with transversal gates.
gapClasses.summary: Willow decoded a distance-5 memory in real time, and Riverlane's decoder answered within 9.6 µs on Rigetti qubits. The decoders the other roadmaps need are harder: correlated decoding for transversal gates, qLDPC surgery decoding and feed-forward for magic-state injection inside one logical cycle all still run offline or in simulation.

evidence.t: Willow decoded a distance-5 memory with 63 µs average latency at 1.1 µs cycles, without backlog.
IBM's Relay-BP decodes the gross code on AMD FPGAs but has not decoded a live logical experiment.
IonQ's 408-logical-qubit real-time decoding result is a simulation on one CPU.
Correlated decoding of transversal circuits is published in simulation, with a faster variant in 2025.

gapClasses.why: Latency depends on code, noise, hardware and windowing, so published results are not comparable; correlated syndromes from transversal gates and non-local checks break the locality fast decoders rely on.
gapClasses.close: Live decoding of high-rate logic with no backlog over 10⁶ rounds, and feed-forward of an injected T gate inside one cycle.
gapClasses.partners: Decoder suppliers (Riverlane, NVIDIA, IBM with AMD), control-stack makers (Qblox, Quantum Machines, Berkeley Lab's QubiC), hardware teams on each modality, and DOE's V&V testbed, which evaluates control-stack integration.

gapClasses.name: A shared yardstick
gapClasses.line: Each company reports logical performance in its own units, and post-selection is reported inconsistently.
gapClasses.summary: Google reports logical error per cycle with open data, QuEra moved to operation budgets, IBM counts gates on logical qubits and IonQ reports breakeven after discarding up to three quarters of shots. DOE will agree a methodology with each awardee, DARPA's QBI IV&V milestone is due in December 2026 and IEEE P7131 is not ratified, so no cross-vendor protocol yet exists.

evidence.t: Google's below-threshold experiment released its data; none of the other three companies has released raw QEC data.
Helios ran 48 error-corrected and up to 94 error-detected logical qubits, a split that depends on how detection is counted.
A 2024 claim of logical error up to 800× below physical drew scrutiny over post-selection.
QuEra replaced logical-qubit counts with operation budgets in June 2026.

gapClasses.why: Hard operations, post-selection, leakage and loss need common definitions, and vendors have reasons to report in their own units.
gapClasses.close: One open protocol for hard operations completed reliably, logical error per operation and discard rate, run by a third-party laboratory on two modalities.
gapClasses.partners: DOE V&V laboratories (Sandia, Berkeley Lab, Oak Ridge) leading teams with at least two vendors per modality, together with DARPA QBI and IEEE P7131.

gapClasses.name: Noise that appears at scale
gapClasses.line: Leakage, loss, bursts and drift are handled one platform at a time, and calibration still needs people.
gapClasses.summary: Transmon leakage removal cut leakage to about 0.1%, and a 3,000-atom array ran for two hours with reloading. Yet IonQ's 2026 qLDPC run discarded 19% to 75% of shots on detected leakage, correlated phase-error bursts recur about once a minute in a gap-engineered transmon array, the largest closed-loop calibration results are at hundreds of qubits, and no learned model forecasts logical error with calibrated uncertainty at a new scale.

evidence.t: Correlated phase-error bursts occur about once every 71 s on average in a gap-engineered superconducting array.
IonQ discarded 19% to 75% of shots for detected leakage in its 2026 qLDPC experiment.
Google's reinforcement-learning control held a distance-7 memory at 7.72×10⁻⁴ per cycle with up to 3.5× better drift stability.
The largest autonomous bring-up found is a 112-qubit processor.

gapClasses.why: Each error type has a different origin and detection method, correlated and non-Markovian noise is hard to identify from syndromes alone, and calibration dependency graphs do not obviously scale linearly.
gapClasses.close: Discard rates under 10%, a decoder response to bursts on hardware, logical-error forecasts within 2× on held-out circuits, and autonomous calibration above 1,000 qubits.
gapClasses.partners: Hardware makers releasing raw syndrome data (only Google does today), noise-learning groups (Sydney, Duke, ETH, Delft), loss and erasure specialists (Harvard, AWS, UW–Madison), Fermilab's SQMS for materials and burst physics, and AI-for-calibration teams (NVIDIA, Quantum Machines).

gapClasses.name: Workloads nobody has costed comparably
gapClasses.line: No DOE science instance has been compiled to 100 logical qubits and 10⁵ hard operations with agreeing estimates.
gapClasses.summary: The RFA asks every applicant for hard and easy operation counts and wall-clock time for a demonstrator, and the SCAC report asks for an end-to-end calculation within 24 hours. Published estimates for DOE-relevant problems sit well above that scale, estimates for the same molecule differ by orders of magnitude across architectures, and no study reconciles three independent tools on one target.

evidence.t: Google's estimate for FeMoco needs about four million physical qubits and under four days.
IonQ's compiled elliptic-curve blueprint needs 1,457 logical qubits and 39 million logical Toffoli gates.
CUDA-Q Logical is the first compiler front end retargeted to more than one logical-code backend.
DARPA QBI's IV&V milestone, the first formal audit route for estimates, is due in December 2026.

gapClasses.why: Each tool encodes noise models, codes and compilation differently, classical baselines keep improving, and compilers are optimized one modality at a time.
gapClasses.close: One instance per DOE science target at First-generation scale, three estimators agreeing within 2×, and one compiled workflow run within 24 hours.
gapClasses.partners: DOE science programs and laboratory domain scientists in chemistry, materials, fusion, nuclear and particle physics, working with resource-estimator builders, cross-modality compiler groups (UCLA, NVIDIA, Microsoft) and DARPA QBI's IV&V.

gapClasses.name: Logic across modules
gapClasses.line: Two-module links work; no fault-tolerant operation has spanned three or more modules.
gapClasses.summary: IBM's Starling is built from linked modules in 2029, IonQ links two chips in 2028 and Google's million-qubit milestone needs links. Today the best inter-module gates are physical, not logical, and multi-module fault tolerance exists only in simulation.

evidence.t: Oxford teleported a CZ gate between ion-trap modules at 86.2% fidelity.
An Argonne and Chicago two-chip router reached 96% average CZ fidelity across all qubit pairs.
Duke and IonQ entangled trapped-ion qubits across three nodes.
Threshold theory tolerates about 10% link error against 1% in the bulk.

gapClasses.why: Link rates and fidelities differ by orders of magnitude across modalities, multi-module control must be synchronized, and decoders have to span modules in real time.
gapClasses.close: A fault-tolerant logical operation across three real modules, with inter-module logical error within 2× of intra-module.
gapClasses.partners: Q-NEXT at Argonne as a neutral interconnect hub, networking groups (Oxford, Duke, Delft, Harvard with AWS), and the companies whose roadmaps depend on links (IBM, IonQ, Google).

IBM.name: IBM Quantum
IBM.philosophy: Modular superconducting machines on high-rate codes
IBM.lead: IBM has the most complete fault-tolerance plan of the four, with a named system for every year from 2026 to 2029. It reaches DOE's First-generation scale with Starling in 2029, a year after DOE's evaluation, and every step depends on logic on gross-code memories that has not yet run on hardware.

conclusions.h: The most complete plan in DOE units, dated a year after DOE's evaluation.
conclusions.t: IBM's roadmap names each step from Kookaburra (2026) and Cockatoo (2027) to Starling (2029, 200 logical qubits and 10⁸ gates) and Blue Jay (2033, 2,000 logical qubits). Starling is the first IBM system at DOE's First-generation scale, a year after the September 2028 evaluation, and IBM has not said what share of Starling's 10⁸ gates are hard operations.

conclusions.h: The plan rests on gross-code logic that has not run on hardware.
conclusions.t: IBM's bivariate-bicycle codes hold 12 logical qubits in 288 physical qubits in simulation, about a tenth of a comparable surface code, and IBM-led theory (extractors, gauging, bridging codes) defines a logical instruction set for them. No hardware logical memory on these codes has been published; Loon, the first test chip, was due for assembly at the end of 2025, and Kookaburra was due in 2026.

conclusions.h: Strongest where DOE's science and integration goals meet today's hardware.
conclusions.t: Three of the SCAC report's state-of-the-art examples ran on IBM Heron processors: a 12,635-atom protein-ligand complex, fusion-blanket molten salts and KCuF₃ spectra checked against neutron data. IBM hardware sits beside Fugaku at RIKEN and on site at Cleveland Clinic and RPI, IBM is in Oak Ridge's user program, and it entered DARPA QBI Stage B in November 2025.

conclusions.h: Decoding is ahead of the logical hardware.
conclusions.t: IBM's Relay-BP decoder runs on AMD FPGAs in under 480 ns, reported a year ahead of IBM's own schedule, but it has not yet decoded a live logical-qubit experiment.

gaps.h: IBM states no hard-operation count.
gaps.t: Starling's 10⁸ gates come without a stated non-Clifford share or magic-state rate, and IBM's first multi-module magic-state injection is planned for 2028. DOE counts hard operations, so IBM's roadmap cannot yet be read against the 10³ and 10⁵ hard-operation tiers.

gaps.h: The first hardware logic on gross codes is still ahead.
gaps.t: No logical memory or logical measurement on a bivariate-bicycle code has been published on IBM hardware. Every later IBM milestone depends on it, which makes the first Kookaburra results the most informative IBM data point for 2026–27.

gaps.h: No open syndrome data and no published treatment of leakage on long-range couplers.
gaps.t: IBM has released no raw QEC syndrome data and no paper treats leakage, loss or bursts in its long-range c-coupler circuits, which differ from the local circuits where leakage handling has been shown. Outside noise-learning groups cannot model these circuits without data.

gaps.h: No wall-clock estimate for a Starling workload.
gaps.t: IBM has published no logical cycle time or wall-clock estimate for a workload on Starling, while the RFA asks for wall-clock time per demonstrator and the SCAC report asks for an end-to-end calculation within 24 hours.

gaps.h: Lower-level access is narrowing.
gaps.t: IBM's documentation says pulse-level control was deprecated in 2025, while DOE asks for access to architectures, control interfaces and diagnostics so that national-laboratory staff can verify claims.

Leads qLDPC gadget theory; Kookaburra LPU module targeted for 2026, no hardware logic yet

Runs a public, crowdsourced classical-vs-quantum tracker

No IBM-led verification work found; Qiskit itself is a third-party verification target.

Google.name: Google Quantum AI
Google.philosophy: Prove each layer of error correction, then scale
Google.lead: Google has the best measured logical memories and publishes its data, but its roadmap is defined by error targets rather than dates. Milestones 3 to 6 are undated, so its path cannot yet be placed against DOE's September 2028 evaluation.

conclusions.h: The best measured logical memories, with data released.
conclusions.t: Willow ran a distance-7 surface-code memory below threshold at 0.143% error per cycle with Λ = 2.14, and in 2026 reinforcement-learning control lowered the error to 0.077% per cycle. The 2024 experiment's data are public on Zenodo, which none of the other three companies has matched.

conclusions.h: A roadmap defined by error targets, not dates.
conclusions.t: Google's six milestones run from beyond-classical computation to about a million physical qubits, with Milestone 3 a long-lived logical qubit at about 10⁻⁶ error and Milestone 5 about 100 logical qubits. Milestones 3 to 6 are undated, and the stated horizon is commercially relevant machines by the end of the decade.

conclusions.h: Leading on magic states and real-time decoding at small scale.
conclusions.t: Google introduced magic-state cultivation and showed it on hardware in 2025 (state fidelity 0.9999, keeping 8% of attempts), and its real-time decoder kept pace with a distance-5 memory at 1.1 µs cycles with 63 µs average latency. Multi-qubit logic is thin: the best result is lattice-surgery teleportation between two color-code qubits at 86.5% to 90.7% fidelity.

conclusions.h: The least open to DOE's facility model, the most open in software.
conclusions.t: No on-premises or HPC-center deployment of a Google machine was found, hardware access runs through a partner-only Willow Early Access Program, and Google is not in Oak Ridge's user program; its DOE link found here is algorithm work with Sandia. Its open software (Cirq, Stim, Qualtran) is the most widely used QEC tooling.

gaps.h: Milestones are not expressed in DOE units or dates.
gaps.t: Google has not converted Milestones 3 to 6 into logical-qubit and hard-operation targets with dates, which the RFA asks applicants to do.

gaps.h: One or two logical qubits on hardware so far.
gaps.t: Hardware holds one or two logical qubits; 100 logical qubits at about 10⁻⁶ (Milestone 5) needs lattice surgery and decoding at a scale that has not been shown.

gaps.h: Cultivation's acceptance rate at workload scale.
gaps.t: Cultivation kept 8% of attempts on hardware. At First-generation scale the acceptance rate and qubit-rounds per accepted state set how many factories must run in parallel, and no Google estimate ties these to a 10⁵-hard-operation workload.

gaps.h: Bursts during a 24-hour run.
gaps.t: Rare correlated error events about once an hour cap Willow's repetition codes near 10⁻¹⁰, phase-error bursts occur about once every 71 s in a gap-engineered array, and no decoder or scheduler response has been demonstrated, which matters for a run that must finish within a day.

gaps.h: Narrow hardware science and few laboratory partnerships.
gaps.t: Google's hardware science covers (2+1)D lattice-gauge dynamics and spin transport, and no DOE-laboratory hardware collaboration beyond algorithm work with Sandia was found.

QuEra.name: QuEra Computing
QuEra.philosophy: Move the atoms, compute with transversal logic
QuEra.lead: QuEra is the only company that dates First-generation scale inside 2028, and its hardware evidence on logical operations is the strongest of the four, much of it led by Harvard. Runtime at millisecond-scale cycles and the hard-operation share of its operation budgets are the open questions.

conclusions.h: The only roadmap that dates First-generation scale inside 2028.
conclusions.t: Libra, planned for 2028 on Amazon Braket, targets over 256 logical qubits at 10⁻⁶ error, and a gigaquop system with over 1,000 logical qubits at 10⁻⁹ follows in 2028–29 for internal use first. QuEra has not stated Libra's runtime or what share of a megaquop is hard operations.

conclusions.h: The strongest hardware evidence on logical operations, much of it Harvard-led.
conclusions.t: With Harvard and MIT, QuEra-linked teams ran 48 error-detected logical qubits with 48 logical CCZ gates (2023), distilled logical magic states from 95.1% to 99.4% fidelity with post-selection, and ran a distance-5 surface code at 0.62% error per round, 2.14 times below distance 3, in a four-round circuit on up to 448 atoms.

conclusions.h: Atom loss handled better than anywhere else, with slow cycles.
conclusions.t: A 3,000-atom array ran continuously for over two hours with reloading, and loss-aware decoding is published. Entangling gates take 270 ns but error-correction cycles are millisecond-scale, so the wall-clock time of a 10⁵-operation workload is the central open question.

conclusions.h: A plan that changed in public.
conclusions.t: The January 2024 roadmap promised 100 logical qubits in 2026; it was replaced by Libra and the gigaquop plan, and in June 2026 QuEra moved from logical-qubit counts to operation budgets (megaquop and gigaquop).

gaps.h: Libra's 10⁻⁶ is not defined.
gaps.t: QuEra has not said whether Libra's 10⁻⁶ is per operation or per round, or whether it is measured with or without post-selection.

gaps.h: No wall-clock estimates.
gaps.t: QuEra has published no wall-clock estimate at millisecond-scale cycles, which the RFA asks for per workload.

gaps.h: The non-Clifford share of a megaquop is not stated.
gaps.t: Operation budgets aggregate all operations; DOE's tiers count hard operations, so the share of non-Clifford operations decides how a megaquop maps onto the 10⁵ tier.

gaps.h: Correlated decoding has not run in real time on hardware.
gaps.t: Transversal gates need correlated decoding, published in simulation with a faster 2025 variant; Libra cites NVIDIA for fast decoding, but no real-time hardware run has been shown.

gaps.h: No open data or syndrome-based noise learning.
gaps.t: No raw QEC data release and no syndrome-based noise-learning work from QuEra were found.

fit.h: 2023 logical-qubit IQP sampling remains the reference result

IonQ.name: IonQ
IonQ.philosophy: Electronic qubit control on a manufacturable chip
IonQ.lead: IonQ's dates are the most aggressive of the four, with about 800 logical qubits in 2027 on paper, and it is building the integration layer early. Its public hardware evidence is a post-selected qLDPC memory; no logical gate or magic state has been shown on IonQ hardware.

conclusions.h: The most aggressive dates of the four.
conclusions.t: IonQ lists 12 logical qubits in 2026, about 800 logical qubits on 10,000 physical qubits in 2027, 1,600 logical qubits on two linked chips in 2028 and up to 80,000 logical qubits on 2,000,000 physical qubits by 2030, with logical error below 10⁻¹² at the end. On paper the 2027 step exceeds DOE's 100-logical-qubit First-generation tier.

conclusions.h: Public hardware evidence is memory, not logic.
conclusions.t: In 2026 IonQ reported qLDPC memories on a 40-ion chain at about breakeven, encoding two to four logical qubits per block after discarding 19% to 75% of shots for detected leakage. Larger codes did not yet outperform smaller ones, and no logical gate or magic-state preparation on IonQ hardware has been published.

conclusions.h: The 99.99% gate is a two-ion result.
conclusions.t: IonQ's record two-qubit fidelity of 99.99% (October 2025) came from a two-ion electronic-control prototype measured with subspace randomized benchmarking, while production Forte systems report 99.3% to 99.5%. Superion 256 launched in September 2026 with deliveries in 2027 and no array-wide data yet.

Forte Enterprise runs on site at EPB in Chattanooga, IonQ is one of four platforms in Oak Ridge's user program, Superion 256 is sold to Florida International University and NVIDIA's NVAQC for 2027, and IonQ acquired the SkyWater foundry in 2026. It published a fully compiled elliptic-curve blueprint and the Walking Cat architecture, both in simulation.

gaps.h: No logic or magic states on hardware.
gaps.t: No public result shows logical gates or magic-state preparation on IonQ systems, so DOE's 10³ (Prototype) and 10⁵ (First-generation) hard-operation tiers have no IonQ hardware baseline.

gaps.h: Logical-qubit counts without hard-operation targets.
gaps.t: The roadmap lists logical-qubit counts but no hard-operation target and no date for a fault-tolerant algorithm on 100 logical qubits, so it cannot be compared directly with DOE's September 2028 evaluation.

gaps.h: Shot discards far from the roadmap's error target.
gaps.t: The best public logical error is about 1% to 3.5% per logical qubit per cycle after discarding 19% to 75% of shots, against a roadmap target below 10⁻⁷ for 2026 and 2027.

gaps.h: Two overhead figures that do not match.
gaps.t: The roadmap's 12.5 physical qubits per logical qubit (10,000 to 800) differs from the Walking Cat dense configuration, about 23 physical per logical (2,514 for 110), and IonQ has not reconciled the two.

gaps.h: Array-scale fidelity and ion transport are unshown.
gaps.t: The 256- and 10,000-qubit chips have no published array-wide gate fidelity, and Walking Cat needs ion transport across about 2,500 qubits where QCCD operation has been shown on devices of up to 98.

fit.h: No public IonQ work on certifying beyond-classical results found.

community.title: The four companies and the wider community
community.lead: National laboratories, universities and other companies produce most of the theory, tools and independent checks that the four company roadmaps depend on. This page maps who does what, where each group leads, and where coverage is thin.
conclusions: Universities write most of the theory the company roadmaps run on.

The logical instruction sets for high-rate codes come largely from university groups: code surgery and extractors from Oxford, Sydney and MIT (with IBM), high-rate surgery from Caltech and Chicago, qLDPC magic-state factories from Yale and Harvard, transversal non-Clifford codes from Berkeley and near-optimal atom-array compilers from UCLA. Most of this work is simulation; the hardware to test it sits with companies.
National laboratories are referees, integrators and hosts rather than builders of logical qubits.

DOE's $45M V&V testbed call requires a laboratory lead with at least two outside collaborators, Oak Ridge's user program gives access to IBM, IQM, IonQ and Quantinuum hardware, Sandia's Quantum Performance Laboratory supplies benchmarking methods, and Oak Ridge, Los Alamos and Sandia co-author science and resource studies with IBM, QuEra and Google. None of the ten laboratories reviewed operates a logical-qubit machine of its own, and Sandia's open trapped-ion testbed is scheduled to close after fiscal 2026.
Other companies hold several of the strongest logical-qubit results.

Quantinuum's 98-qubit Helios ran 48 error-corrected and up to 94 error-detected logical qubits (February 2026) and a logical non-Clifford gate below physical error; Microsoft and Atom Computing entangled 24 logical qubits and ran circuits on up to 28; Infleqtion reported 30 logical qubits on 80 atoms in September 2026. Several of these rely on error detection or post-selection, which is why a shared reporting convention matters.
Neutral suppliers are forming around decoding and control.

Riverlane's FPGA decoder completes a round in under a microsecond and is deployed with several hardware makers and Oak Ridge, NVIDIA's NVQLink reports 3.96 µs GPU round trips and launched with 17 hardware builders and nine national laboratories, and open control stacks from Berkeley Lab and Quantum Machines give outsiders a way into the real-time loop.
The thinnest coverage sits where DOE's tiers bind.

Across all groups reviewed, the weakest areas are sustained magic-state production, logic between high-rate code blocks on hardware, verified decoders and compilers, and cross-tool resource estimates for DOE science targets. Among the four companies only Google releases raw QEC data, which limits what university noise-learning groups can test.

labs.name: Fermilab (SQMS)
labs.focus: Superconducting-qubit materials and coherence, and SRF-cavity multimode and qudit hardware.
labs.summary: Fermilab leads the SQMS center, which works on the physical layer beneath fault tolerance. Reported results include niobium transmons with tantalum capping (median T1 above 300 microseconds, maxima near 600) and ultracoherent superconducting radio-frequency cavities with single-photon lifetimes of 15 to 21 milliseconds that serve as multi-level (qudit) registers with error-resilient control. These are enabling-hardware results, not logical-qubit demonstrations, so they bear mainly on the trust milestone (lower physical error for below-threshold memories) and on bosonic or qudit encodings. SQMS was renewed in November 2025 with $125 million over five years.
programs: Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center (SQMS), a Fermilab-led DOE National QIS Research Center renewed in Nov 2025 within the $625M five-center award
partners: Northwestern University (eight co-authors on the 2024 niobium-encapsulation paper in npj Quantum Information, including Mark Hersam and Jens Koch)
Rigetti Computing (ten co-authors on the same 2024 encapsulation paper)

works.what: Tantalum-capped niobium transmons reach median T1 above 300 microseconds and maxima up to 600 microseconds, lowering the physical-error floor under below-threshold memories.
Two-mode SRF cavity platform with single-photon lifetimes of 20.6 ms and 15.6 ms, Fock-state preparation above 95% up to N=20 and error-resilient control, as a basis for qudit and bosonic encodings.

labs.name: Argonne (Q-NEXT)
labs.focus: Quantum interconnects, networking and materials integration; Argonne and SLAC Quantum Foundries.
labs.summary: Argonne leads Q-NEXT, whose November 2025 renewal ($125M over five years) centers on quantum communication, sensing and materials integration, supported by the Argonne and SLAC Quantum Foundries and Argonne's light-source and computing facilities. The most relevant fault-tolerance output is modular hardware: a University of Chicago and Argonne two-chip superconducting processor with an all-to-all reconfigurable router (96% average controlled-Z fidelity), which bears on inter-module fault tolerance (P12) and the scale milestone. Q-NEXT also published a 2022 interconnect roadmap.
programs: Q-NEXT, Argonne-led DOE National QIS Research Center, renewed Nov 4 2025 ($125M over five years; $25M in FY2026)
access: Argonne and SLAC Quantum Foundries, Advanced Photon Source, Center for Nanoscale Materials and Argonne Leadership Computing Facility, named as Q-NEXT key facilities: https://www.anl.gov/article/argonneled-qnext-quantum-center-renewed-for-five-years

works.what: Two-chip modular superconducting processor with a reconfigurable all-to-all router reaches 96% average CZ fidelity across all qubit pairs and 88.15% and 75.18% fidelity for three- and four-qubit entangled states, a hardware step toward multi-module fault tolerance.

labs.name: Brookhaven (C2QA)
labs.focus: Co-design of superconducting, neutral-atom and diamond-based quantum systems: materials, modular architectures, error correction, algorithms and software.
labs.summary: Brookhaven leads C2QA, a 28-institution center that pairs materials work, notably tantalum superconducting circuits with coherence above one millisecond, with architecture and error-correction co-design across superconducting, neutral-atom and diamond platforms. Listed C2QA outputs from 2023-24 include real-time error correction beyond break-even, erasure-detected dual-rail cavity qubits, a sliding-window decoder for noisy-syndrome qLDPC decoding and a lattice-surgery architecture for surface codes. These map to the trust and logic milestones and to problems P03, P04 and P10. C2QA was renewed in November 2025.
programs: Co-design Center for Quantum Advantage (C2QA), Brookhaven-led DOE National QIS Research Center, renewed Nov 4 2025 ($125M over five years; director Charles Black)
access: Bosonic Qiskit, C2QA's bosonic-simulation extension of Qiskit (2022 release): https://arxiv.org/html/2209.11153v2

works.what: Improves sliding-window decoding of quantum LDPC codes under noisy syndrome measurements, a step toward real-time decoding of high-rate codes.

QuIRC, a C2QA-funded routing card for lattice surgery between surface-code modules on separate chips in one refrigerator (Princeton, UMass Amherst and PNNL authors): ancilla patch size down by up to 77.8% against a single chip.
Real-time error correction beyond break-even, listed in C2QA's publications and highlighted in its 2025 renewal as the first quantum error correction significantly beyond break-even.
Demonstrates erasure detection for a dual-rail qubit in a superconducting cavity, a loss-aware route toward lower logical error.
Separates loss channels in tantalum superconducting circuits; C2QA's renewal reports tantalum-based qubits with coherence times above one millisecond.

labs.name: Lawrence Berkeley (QSA, AQT, NERSC)
labs.focus: Multi-platform quantum systems (QSA), superconducting testbed and characterization (AQT), and HPC-linked quantum access (NERSC).
labs.summary: Berkeley Lab contributes through three vehicles. QSA, which it leads (renewed 2025 with $125M), targets 1,000-fold gains in computational power by 2030 across neutral-atom, trapped-ion and superconducting platforms. The Advanced Quantum Testbed supports superconducting-circuit research and benchmarking and characterization methods, relevant to V&V-style performance claims (P15). NERSC provides HPC and cloud access to quantum hardware, including an IBM Quantum Innovation Center and a 2026 call for neutral-atom access, relevant to the bridge milestone.
programs: Quantum Systems Accelerator (QSA), Berkeley Lab-led, renewed 2025 ($125M, $25M in year one; director Bert de Jong, deputy Christopher DeRose of Sandia)
NERSC quantum access (IBM Quantum Innovation Center; QIS@Perlmutter)
